POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Tue, 06 Oct 2026 14:19:43 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.9 Greens probe conduct complaint against Deputy Leader Mothin Ali https://www.politico.eu/article/greens-probe-conduct-complaint-against-deputy-leader-mothin-ali/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 06 Oct 2026 14:05:44 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9113633 LONDON — The Green Party is reviewing a complaint against its deputy leader following an alleged altercation at a local meeting, two people with knowledge of the procedure have told POLITICO.

The probe into Mothin Ali’s conduct follows a report by Leeds outlet the Exchange of a public dispute between the deputy leader and a member of his local party at a meeting last month.

According to minutes of the Leeds Green Party group meeting, reviewed by POLITICO, Ali “snatched” a phone from an attendee and “threw the phone onto the floor” after the person “attempted to take an image with Mothin in the background.” 

Both were then asked to leave, the Sept. 15 minutes state. The Green Party told the Exchange at the time that it disputed “this incomplete account” of the alleged altercation.

A complaint about Ali was lodged with the Green Party a week later, according to a party official, who was granted anonymity like others in this article to discuss a sensitive matter. 

The deputy leader has not been suspended by the party while the allegations are under review. A Green Party spokesperson said: “We do not comment on internal matters.” Ali declined to comment, instead directing POLITICO to the party press office.

The first party official referenced above told POLITICO any decision on whether or not to suspend Ali is expected to take about five weeks, in part due to the Greens’ Brighton conference — which Ali attended — slowing what is normally a shorter process.

The second person familiar with the process, an ally of Ali, said the deputy leader had been “under a lot of pressure” and that the party had failed to support him in the face of attacks.

Ali — one of two Green Party deputy leaders — said in a statement on X last month that he had “been subjected to a sustained series of allegations, complaints, leaks and personal attacks” since standing to become deputy leader, and argued that some of these had been “explicitly racist and Islamophobic.”

He told the party’s Brighton conference in a speech Saturday that internal disagreement “must never mean tolerating racism, misogyny, homophobia or intimidation inside our own movement.”

The row comes at a sensitive moment for the Green Party, which has been posing a left-wing challenge to Britain’s Labour government under Leader Zack Polanski, but seen some support drift away amid the rise of new Prime Minister Andy Burnham. 

Ali has spent the weekend in Brighton rebutting rumors that he could pose a leadership challenge to Polanski at the party’s next election — not due to take place for another year. 

Speaking to the BBC over the weekend, Ali said that Polanski — who is trying to win a seat in Parliament at the Holborn and St Pancras by-election this week — had his “full support.”

]]> en Jailed Albanian mayor uses AI avatar to make deepfake speech https://www.politico.eu/article/jailed-albanian-mayor-erion-veliaj-uses-ai-avatar-to-make-deepfake-speech/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 06 Oct 2026 13:36:46 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro-free&p=9114164 TIRANA, Albania — Tirana Mayor Erion Veliaj has caused a stir with a video pledge of free school lunches for all the capital’s children. There’s one problem: Veliaj is currently in prison, and the blue-suited figure making the heartfelt announcement is AI-generated.

In an Instagram post on his official profile labeled as AI-generated, the video likeness of the 46-year-old appears in front of the Albanian and municipal flags, listing his achievements in office while reiterating his promise of free school lunches for the city’s kids. 

“I made another commitment that I will never forget: food in schools,” says the Veliaj clone. “I will keep this promise even from this cell where they have locked me up.”

Veliaj has been in prison in the coastal city of Durres since early 2025 amid investigations over allegations of corruption and financial crimes. He denies any wrongdoing. 

“My hostage situation has been going on for 20 months, and I can only greet you with artificial intelligence,” his avatar says. “I will continue to work even from the cell … I hug you with longing, you and your wonderful children.”

After his arrest and imprisonment, snap elections for Tirana were scheduled last November, but were canceled at the last minute after a Constitutional Court ruling found he could not be dismissed outside of normal democratic processes. Veliaj has delegated duties to several deputy mayors while he is incarcerated, but remains the official mayor of the city until municipal elections take place in the first half of 2027.

This isn’t the first time imprisoned politicians have used AI to communicate with the public. In 2023, Pakistan’s jailed former leader Imran Khan used an AI deepfake to urge citizens to vote for his Tehreek-e-Insaf party during elections.

Then in July, an AI-generated avatar of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro appeared at the launch of his son Flavio’s presidential campaign. Bolsonaro is under house arrest and barred from participating in election-related discourse or events.

This is also not the first time Albanian officials have been provocative with AI. In autumn 2025, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama introduced the country to Diella, the world’s first AI-powered virtual minister, who was officially appointed to the government cabinet and tasked with rooting out corruption in tender and procurement processes.

A few months after the appointment, Diella came under fire when the woman whose likeness was used for her face and voice objected to the use of her image for a ministerial position.

]]> en Police arrest another British man in RAF Fairford investigation https://www.politico.eu/article/police-arrest-another-british-man-in-raf-fairford-investigation/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 06 Oct 2026 13:02:11 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9114380 LONDON — A seventh man has been arrested as part of an investigation into the suspected terror plot around the RAF Fairford airbase, Britain’s Counter Terrorism Policing said on Tuesday.

The statement said that a 22-year-old British man was arrested on suspicion of the preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006.

This is the seventh arrest in the live investigation into events surrounding a suspected terror plot near the RAF Fairford airbase, which has been used by the United States to conduct defensive strikes against Iran.

Five British men were arrested on Sunday, 27 September, on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and preparation of a terrorist act, after police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the airbase. No improvised explosive devices were found in the vehicles, but investigators recovered a quantity of petrol.

On Thursday, Counter Terrorism Policing arrested a 25-year-old British-Iranian man for the same offense as part of investigations. All six men were later released on bail.

On Sunday, the Pentagon confirmed that the U.S. had withdrawn all B-1 bombers from the airbase. The following day, U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters that the United States had known of a “threat” which led them to move the bombers.

Counter-terror police — supported by the MI5 intelligence service — are currently investigating “possible foreign state involvement” as part of their enquiries.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government believes “Iran to have played a part” in the incident.

]]> en EU Parliament spat as MEP challenges Metsola’s claims over Israeli flag https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-parliament-spat-as-mep-rima-hassan-challenges-roberta-metsola-claims-over-israeli-flag/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 06 Oct 2026 12:51:34 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9113720 STRASBOURG — French EU lawmaker Rima Hassan pushed back Tuesday against European Parliament President Roberta Metsola’s claim that Israeli and EU flags had been knocked over.

Metsola said before Tuesday’s votes that a member of the Parliament had been filmed on Monday evening “apparently damaging” an exhibition marking the Oct. 7 attacks.

According to Metsola, they were seen throwing an Israeli flag to the ground and dropping a flagpole, and an EU flag was also knocked over. She said both flags were left on the floor.

“We take this extremely seriously,” Metsola said, adding that “all appropriate steps” were being taken and that the individual concerned would have the right to give their side of the story.

She said Parliament could not tolerate property damage or actions that could be seen as intimidation.

“At a time of rising global antisemitism, we owe it to Europe’s Jewish community to ensure that when they look to us, they see that this is their house too,” Metsola said.

Metsola did not announce any sanctions or name the individual. A spokesperson for the president said the procedures under consideration could include sanctions, while a Parliament spokesperson said the next steps included hearing from the lawmaker concerned.

Hassan, a lawmaker from the France Unbowed party and the European Parliament’s Left group, responded from the floor minutes later, accusing Metsola of making comments that were “factually false.”

Hassan said the exhibition had been organized in partnership with the Israeli embassy and defended her opposition to the presence of the Israeli flag in the Parliament, comparing it to displaying a Russian flag given Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

A Parliament spokesperson did not confirm whether the event was organized in conjunction with the Israeli embassy, saying the center-right European People’s Party had arranged it.

She also alleged that the event featured a map depicting a “Greater Israel” and that organizers had told her the Palestinian people and Palestine do not exist.

Those claims could not immediately be independently verified.

The exchange followed accusations on Monday night from French center-right lawmaker François-Xavier Bellamy, who said Hassan had thrown both the Israeli and European flags to the ground and called for her to be sanctioned. Parliament Vice-President Pina Picierno also accused Hassan of trampling the flags.

Hassan confirmed in a statement that she had removed the Israeli flag from its stand, but the EU flag had inadvertently fallen over due to a loss of balance. She added that neither was damaged and that she had written to Metsola to set out her version of events.

“I did not touch the European flag,” she also told the chamber.

The exhibition was organized ahead of the third anniversary of the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attacks on Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.

Under Parliament’s rules, sanctions for serious breaches can range from a reprimand to the loss of daily allowances or temporary suspension from some parliamentary activities.

]]> en France’s Le Pen unveils economic platform stuffed with cuts — but few new ideas https://www.politico.eu/article/le-pen-unveils-economic-platform-stuffed-with-eye-watering-cuts-but-few-new-ideas/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 06 Oct 2026 12:09:23 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9112943 PARIS — Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen offered her usual recipe for pulling the French economy from the brink of a sovereign debt crisis when she presented her economic platform on Tuesday: curbing immigration, cutting France’s contributions to the European Union and slashing red tape.

“If the French do not choose a political about-face, France will head toward default,” Le Pen said at a lengthy press conference at her National Rally party’s headquarters.

Le Pen spent much of her opening speech attacking what she called President Emmanuel Macron’s “disastrous track record” on the economy. Seated alongside her was party president Jordan Bardella, who during the press conference again denied allegations that he sent antisemitic remarks on Facebook Messenger as a teenager. Bardella accused the outlet that published the report, Mediapart, of trying to dig up dirt on him by asking former classmates of his to send screenshots of private conversations when he was as young as 12.

“I won’t accuse you of perversity, others will judge, but it doesn’t look like your little operation is having an impact in the country,” he said.

Le Pen, the front-runner in the race to replace Macron next year, let Bardella do most of the talking in his defense. For her, the event was an opportunity to cast herself as a responsible steward of the French economy as France’s debt continues to pile up, growth stagnates and borrowing costs rise. On Tuesday she promised €140 billion in net savings over the course of a five-year presidential term.

“If investors only lend at exorbitant rates, our state and our social system will collapse,” she said.

Le Pen’s proposal to cut €19.5 billion from France’s EU contributions is bound to set up a showdown with Brussels. The party’s counter-budget proposal for 2027 includes an €11.1 billion cut in France’s gross contribution to the bloc as early as next year.

Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a National Rally lawmaker widely seen as a contender for economy minister should Le Pen win next year’s presidential election, said that Le Pen and her party would ramp up pressure for a fundamental rethink of EU priorities rather than just renegotiating the country’s annual contribution.

“We are not only asking for a rebate, we are asking for the cancellation of entire programs,” Tanguy said, citing EU foreign policy initiatives but also EU funds deployed within pre-accession programs.

During past presidential campaigns, Le Pen and the National Rally have been criticized for floating unrealistic and unfunded proposals that lack important details. They’ve also been accused of inflating the savings in some of their proposals — meaning the numbers unveiled Tuesday will likely be heavily scrutinized.

Le Pen said slashing immigration would save €15 billion during the first year of her potential presidency, and €14 billion in the second. She also said reorganizing France’s social security system would bring in €36.7 billion over five years — though in August she proposed lowering the age of retirement to 62 at a cost of €9 billion per year. She also said that streamlining the French pension system would save €15 billion to €20 billion.

She said she would put to a referendum what she called a fiscal “golden rule” — though her proposal differs from what economists traditionally mean by the term.

Le Pen’s version — also outlined in an opinion piece — would instead require successive governments to reduce France’s public debt as a share of gross domestic product each year until it reaches 60 percent — nearly half its current level. In practical terms, France could still run budget deficits, provided they were small enough for the debt burden to keep falling relative to the size of the economy.

Le Pen also said that she planned to introduce a funded component into the pension system, under which a worker’s contributions are invested for their future retirement rather than paying for current retirees — a proposal that had been pushed by the National Rally’s more pro-business wing.

]]> en Former German spy chief arrested for treason and espionage https://www.politico.eu/article/former-german-spy-chief-bnd-arrested-for-treason-and-espionage-august-hanning/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 06 Oct 2026 09:40:33 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9112808 BERLIN — A former chief of Germany’s foreign intelligence service was arrested early Tuesday on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason amounting to potentially one of the greatest intelligence breaches in the country’s post-Cold War history.

An allegedly paid informant who held high positions inside the foreign intelligence agency, or BND, is accused of providing August Hanning — the former head of the agency from 1998 to 2005 — with nearly 2,000 documents, many of them classified, over a period of a dozen years up to 2022, according to the German Federal Prosecutor’s Office.

Hanning is alleged to have used the information to profit as a private consultant, according to prosecutors. In at least one case, prosecutors say Hanning allegedly used classified information to create an assessment for an employee of a foreign intelligence service.

“The accused Hanning is under strong suspicion of espionage constituting treason,” the prosecutors’ statement read.

The allegations amount to a huge embarrassment for Germany’s scandal-plagued foreign intelligence agency. The BND has a history of being infiltrated by other foreign intelligence services — at times making Western spy agencies reluctant to share sensitive information with the agency.

In 2022, authorities arrested former BND department head Carsten L. on suspicion of spying for Russia, charges he denies in a court case that is still ongoing.

The new allegations come at a particularly sensitive moment for the BND as the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz moves to grant it major new powers to hit back at Moscow, giving the agency much broader authority to perpetrate acts of sabotage, conduct offensive cyber operations and carry out espionage more aggressively.

Many questions will now be raised in Germany about how such a massive intelligence breach could have gone on undetected for more than a decade.

The alleged informant accused of having worked with Hanning was identified as Manfred D., Hanning’s former chief of staff. Following Hanning’s departure, Manfred D. went on to serve as chief of staff to several subsequent BND presidents from March 2012 to March 2026, according to prosecutors.

The material Manfred D. provided Hanning was used to brief the agency’s leadership for regular meetings at the chancellery attended by senior officials from ministries and security agencies, according to prosecutors.

Manfred D. is charged with “aiding and abetting attempted treason and espionage in the interest of a foreign power,” according to the prosecutors’ statement.

It was not immediately clear which foreign intelligence service employee Hanning is alleged to have prepared an assessment for using classified information provided by Manfred D.

In addition to that case, Hanning was also allegedly engaged “in an intensive exchange” with a member of another foreign intelligence service over several years, providing “political information” some of which was based on material received from Manfred D., according to prosecutors.

In neither case were Russian or Chinese intelligence agencies involved, according to a German intelligence official granted anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Hanning’s arrest comes one day after Germany’s current BND chief, Martin Jäger, warned in remarks to parliamentarians that the country risks being drawn into a “violent conflict” with Russia as the Kremlin escalates its “shadow war” on Berlin and hits Ukraine with increasing brutality.

At the same time, Jäger welcomed current draft legislation giving his agency new powers to counter the threat posed by the Kremlin. “We will be a different, a new BND,” he said. “We are aware that additional powers entail greater responsibility.”

On Tuesday, however, Jäger was forced to defend his agency amid mounting concerns that the massive intelligence breach had undermined its ability to counter ongoing threats.

“For the BND and for me, there can be no compromises when it comes to internal security,” Jäger said in a statement. “None of my goals, none of my priorities are called into question by this incident.”

That is unlikely to ease concerns among German lawmakers that the BND has suffered serious reputational damage at one of the most sensitive moments in its history, as it prepares to hit back against rising Russian espionage and sabotage.

“The allegations against August Hanning are grave and appalling,” Greens lawmaker Konstantin von Notz, the deputy chairman of the parliamentary committee that oversees intelligence agencies, told WELT. “Any damage caused to the intelligence services must also be identified and investigated both promptly and comprehensively.”

Hans von der Burchard contributed to this report.

This story has been updated.

]]> en Von der Leyen warns against EU budget cuts https://www.politico.eu/article/ursula-von-der-leyen-warns-against-eu-budget-cuts/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 06 Oct 2026 08:22:46 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9112427 European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen cautioned against cuts to the EU’s next seven-year budget in a rebuke to Germany’s calls to dramatically slash spending.

During a speech in the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Tuesday, von der Leyen said that reducing the size of the EU’s common cash pot would undermine critical EU-wide priorities such as competitiveness and energy autonomy.

“I would like to caution against large cuts. It would risk cutting deep into critical priorities that we all together have agreed on,” von der Leyen told MEPs.

The warning comes days before the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the budget talks, is expected to put forward a budget negotiating document with new figures.

Von der Leyen had previously hailed the Commission’s budget proposal for 2028-2034 as “the most ambitious ever proposed.” But Tuesday, as negotiations among governments enter crunch time, she struck a more cautious note.

In a message to Berlin, von der Leyen recalled that the Commission’s budget proposal represents 1.26% of the European Union’s gross national income — a relatively small increase from the current seven-year cash pot.

She also underscored the need to approve “a significant package of new own resources,” which are EU-wide taxes to finance the budget and reduce national contributions to Brussels.

The bloc’s governments are racing to reach an agreement by the end of the year, before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to disrupt the negotiations.

Despite the looming deadline, EU leaders are still far apart over the size of the new budget.

Germany and its allies in Northern Europe have pressured Dublin to make cuts worth hundreds of billions of euros across the board.

But 17 EU countries from Southern and Eastern Europe — led by Italy and Romania — are pushing in the opposite direction. They asked to preserve farmers’ subsidies and regional payouts, known as cohesion policy, in a joint letter last week.

During a separate speech to the European Parliament on Tuesday, Portuguese Prime Minister Luís Montenegro said that “there is no European competitiveness without cohesion, and no European cohesion without competitiveness.”

In a rebuke to the frugals, Montenegro said that Portugal’s contribution to the EU budget as a share of its gross domestic product is higher than that of Germany and other wealthier countries.

“Giving 10 out of 100 is much more than giving 50 out of 1,000,” he told MEPs.

But Germany insists that its budget contributions are too high. In a thinly veiled threat on Monday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that “having no new financial framework is by far the most financially advantageous solution for Germany.”

However, he added that such a scenario would restrict the EU’s ability to act and renewed calls to end the negotiations by the end of the year.

Several European officials believe that Dublin will propose budget cuts exceeding €100 billion. The proposal is expected to be put forward Saturday and be discussed by EU ambassadors Sunday.

This article has been updated.

]]> de Spanish election threatens to blow up Brussels’ political balance https://www.politico.eu/article/spanish-election-threatens-brussels-political-balance-pedro-sanchez-socialists-european-parliament/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 06 Oct 2026 02:18:45 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9110345 BRUSSELS — A defeat for Pedro Sánchez in Spain’s snap election risks destabilizing the EU by putting the Socialists and Democrats on the back foot in Brussels and pushing them into a more confrontational stance.

Sánchez, the only Socialist-aligned leader currently running a large EU country, has provided a center-left counterweight to decisions in a Council largely dominated by the center right. Spain’s lawmakers form the S&D’s largest national delegation in the European Parliament, and when Sánchez strikes a Council deal, Spanish MEPs can usually carry his position through the group, even over internal opposition.

A change of government in Madrid would disrupt that arrangement, senior S&D lawmakers told POLITICO. Polls suggest that the country will vote in an administration led by the center-right People’s Party, which would likely partner with the far-right Vox party.

“There might be a temptation to look more critically at Council positions if there is no [longer] a Socialist prime minister of a large country,” said René Repasi, head of Germany’s SPD delegation in Parliament.

A second senior S&D lawmaker said Sánchez helped “balance” decisions at the leaders’ table and that his absence would unsettle the informal alliance of the S&D, liberals and the center-right European People’s Party that Commission President Ursula von der Leyen relies on to pass legislation.

“If what comes out of the leaders’ table, and the guidelines it gives the Commission, becomes more conservative, it will be less appealing for progressives to feel part of that governing majority,” said the lawmaker, who was granted anonymity to speak about sensitive group matters.

The S&D has lost ground elsewhere in Brussels. Since the 2024 European election shifted Parliament to the right, the EPP has passed some legislation with far-right groups. The Socialists have less representation in national governments and fewer commissioners of their own, fueling repeated tensions and attempts to repair the alliance. With Sánchez gone, the last center-left leaders would be Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and Malta’s Robert Abela — with Magdalena Andersson working to form a government in Sweden.

Spain’s election will sound the starting gun a year of consequential votes across major EU countries, including Italy, Poland and France, where the far-right National Rally is leading the polls ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Far-right forces in Brussels are pressing the EPP to drop its ban on cooperating with them and break with its traditional ties to the S&D. 

Fewer incentives for compromise

The S&D, Parliament’s second-largest group, has repeatedly threatened over the past two years to withdraw support for von der Leyen, with some lawmakers urging a more forceful stance on EU policy.

Spain’s Iratxe García, who leads the group, has so far kept Spanish lawmakers in line. She faces a leadership vote on Oct. 21, though she is broadly expected to keep her post.

Should Sánchez lose his election, all the S&D’s largest national delegations — from Italy, Romania and France — would be in opposition at home. The only S&D parties still in government would be junior partners in Germany and Austria, alongside Denmark’s Social Democrats, whose hardline stance on migration limits their influence in the group.

Without a heavyweight prime minister from a large EU country to keep the S&D in line, von der Leyen would face greater pressure to make more concessions to lawmakers already frustrated by the center-right’s votes with the far right.

“If von der Leyen still delivers on S&D priorities, she will have the support of the group, and if that is not the case, then she will lose the support of the group,” Repasi said. A formal alliance between Spain’s EPP and far-right Vox, he added, “will drive us even more apart.”

The S&D would also have fewer “incentives” to compromise without Sánchez’s presence, the second senior lawmaker said, because the group would have less responsibility for maintaining stability in EU institutions.

“The institutional responsibility to guarantee support for the Commission and stability in the EU institutions will no longer be there,” the lawmaker said. A tougher line would be easier for the center-left “if the EPP continues striking deals with the far right, and the European Commission fails to offer a politically attractive agenda that progressives can sell to their voters.”

One diplomat called the Socialists’ threat to withdraw support for von der Leyen “not credible,” saying it would isolate the group further: “They just feel a need to send a signal to the EPP.” Weakening or firing von der Leyen also runs against the S&D’s interests, the diplomat added, because the EU has moved further to the right since she first took office and “the next person coming in would be much less inclined to work with them.”

Turbulence ahead

Brussels is set to become a battleground between Spain’s two main parties, with the Spanish lawmakers leading the Socialists in Parliament, while their rivals in the EPP form that group’s second-largest national delegation.

The election is also weighing on talks over the EU’s next seven-year budget, known as the Multiannual Financial Framework, which Brussels aims to conclude by the end of the year.

“It’s not going to do any good for the MFF,” a Commission official said, warning that Spain risks dragging its feet during already strained negotiations. The EPP and its allies will try to put debates on Parliament’s agenda to cause discomfort for Sánchez, the official said, likely making the talks more “turbulent.”

Spain’s underlying budget position will not change under a new government, a second diplomat said, but “the election will be distracting” and “won’t incentivize finding compromise.”

The EPP’s Siegfried Mureșan, Parliament’s lead budget negotiator, warned EU countries not to use the election to delay talks ahead of a leaders’ summit in mid-October. “The European Council shall not use the political situation in Spain as an excuse for further delays.”

EPP leader Manfred Weber declined to comment on what a Sánchez defeat could mean for the Socialists’ influence in Brussels, but voiced support for Spain’s opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo.

“Spain’s future is now in the hands of the Spanish people,” he said. “At a time when vision and reform are needed more than ever, the EPP is proud to stand firmly behind Alberto Núñez Feijóo. He has our full support.”

Zoya Sheftalovich and Tim Ross contributed reporting.

Where are the headlines? https://euobserver.com/241274/the-children-of-gaza-are-being-killed-every-day-where-are-the-headlines/ Tue, 06 Oct 2026 13:43:42 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241274 EU governments continue to authorise arms sales to Israel despite rules and the EU treaties that require them to protect children's rights.]]> Every day, children are killed in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Where are the outraged headlines?

The number of children killed in Gaza since Israel started its onslaught, following the Hamas attack on 7 October, 2023, is estimated at more than 21,600. 

The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) says that since the so-called Israel-Hamas ceasefire, an average of “at least” one child a day – 300 children over 300 days – has been killed in the enclave. 

Children, toddlers, and babies are being killed in their homes, schools, hospitals, shelters, and on roads marked by displacement. They are also dying because the basic structures that should protect them – family, healthcare, education, food, water, and refuge – have been systematically destroyed.

Where are the urgent statements from EU and world leaders?

EU governments continue to authorise arms transfers to Israel despite rules which require governments to deny licences where there is a risk that military equipment will be used for serious violations of international humanitarian law. 

Every EU member state is also bound by the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the EU’s own treaty, which requires the union to promote children’s rights. 

Why are these international rules and domestic commitments not being applied to the children of Gaza?

Children rights beyond Ukraine

The EU does care for children. In Ukraine, the EU treats children as individuals rather than statistics: it convenes coalitions, compiles names, traces families, imposes sanctions, creates mechanisms for return and makes the fate of children a central diplomatic demand. 

In her State of the Union address last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen – a proud mother and grandmother – introduced and praised the courage of Sasha, a six-year-old Ukrainian girl who lost a leg in a Russian missile strike in Ukraine but has now returned to her beloved gymnastics.

Von der Leyen quite rightly made the suffering of Ukrainian children intimate and personal. It is more than time she did the same for Palestinian children.

But let’s not only blame political leaders for their indifference, their lack of historical knowledge of Palestine’s occupation and their limited understanding of Palestinian calls for justice. 

Parts of the legacy media must also own up to their responsibility in normalising the abhorrent.

Powerful mainstream media have preferred to “repeat Israeli propaganda and sometimes simply cut and paste IDF press releases” rather than accept the analysis of Palestinian journalists, writers and scholars, writes Bhakti Shringarpure.

Her criticism reflects a wider ongoing discussion on the sourcing and framing of Gaza coverage, with studies spotlighting how Western media has described Israeli suffering by using emotive language around 11 times more often than Palestinian suffering. References to Israel’s “right to defend itself” appear roughly five times as frequently as references to Palestinian rights.

Also, as the immediate shock of the bombardment recedes – but the killing continues – Gaza has dropped down the news cycle. 

Assal Rad,  author of “Don’t Say Palestine: How the Media Manufactured Consent for Genocide”, describes the logic: “The façade of a ceasefire has created the space to cover it less. In reality, the conditions on the ground for Palestinians in Gaza have not changed.”

It is also less politically costly for leaders and media to focus on settler violence and settlement in the occupied West Bank, since it can be described as the work of “extremists” rather than of the Israeli government.

Read more

Belgium abandons Gaza students with university places, as Italy shows evacuations are possible

EU silence

Our lack of a strong reaction to what is happening is Gaza is also the story of how bystander societies can watch, absorb, and rationalise horrors – and move on. 

Additionally, the killing of Palestinian children is preceded by their political “unchilding”, a process which Palestinian scholar Nadera Shalhoub-Kevorkian says begins before the missile falls, when Palestinian children are imagined not as children with futures but as demographic threats, future militants, or extensions of an armed group. 

Their age, instead of guaranteeing greater protection, becomes entangled with suspicion.

Even amid such savage violence, some people are not giving up. 

Their bosses may still look the other way, but EU Staff for Peace, which holds vigils in front of the European Commission and the EU Council every Thursday, has held gatherings to read out the names of children killed in Gaza, thereby according individuality to children whom the political and media systems have reduced to numbers.

Read more

Putin and Netanyahu will be laughing at EU after von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech

As one EU staffer told me: “We only have a time slot of three hours and the last time we only managed to read out the names of children up to three years old. It took us one hour to read out the names of Palestinian babies under one-year old.”

Hind Rajab, who was five, was killed on 29 January 2024 by Israeli fire on the car in which she was trapped. Her body was found 12 days later alongside the bodies of members of her family and two paramedics who had gone to rescue her.

Israel has acknowledged firing on the car but has not admitted that her killing was unlawful, citing an ongoing investigation. In other words, there has been no accountability.

The obscenity is not only that Hind was killed, but that by now the killing of children in Gaza has become a familiar event. 

The shame is that so many of us have constructed a hierarchy in which some children summon the world’s full moral and political force, while others are ignored.

Omar El Akkad, in his seminal book says that “One Day, Everyone Will Have Always Been Against This.” Given the cowardice on display over the last three years, I sometimes wonder if there will ever really be a true global moral reckoning.

]]> AI machine-gun turrets do battle with Russian jet drones for the skies of Kyiv (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,685) https://euobserver.com/241306/ai-machine-gun-turrets-do-battle-with-russian-jet-drones-for-the-skies-of-kyiv-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1685/ Tue, 06 Oct 2026 13:00:10 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241306 The battle for Kyiv's skies aside, Ukraine’s air raids on Russian oil sites saw it boast that over half of Moscow’s refinery capacity was offline, potentially choking fuel supplies far from the front.]]>
  • Russia continues to pressure cities, while the first autonomous counter-drone turrets have been deployed in Kyiv.
  • Ukraine is maintaining pressure on Russia’s oil industry, reporting that it has disabled 51 percent of refinery capacity.
  • Russia still sees a large pocket of encircled Ukrainians in Kharkiv region, but no such pocket exists.
  • Ukraine says it destroyed a Russian Su-34 and Su-35 on the ground. Satellite imagery provides no clear evidence.
  • Maps of the day – Kharkiv region
  • Videos of the day – intense trench fighting; Russians shot down a balloon carrying an FPV drone; Russia has revived the idea of a barrage of tethered balloons; ground drones repelled an FPV drone attack using a counter-drone net – views from both sides.

    • Russia continues to pressure cities. Ukraine has begun testing AI-controlled machine-gun turrets in them. The new autonomous weapon is intended to protect key sites from drone attacks, typically bridges and similar infrastructure. Air force spokesperson Yuri Ihnat said on Monday that the AI turrets, which receive information from other air-defence components, had achieved their first shoot-downs, including of Geran-5 drones.

    Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky reported on Saturday, before Ihnat’s announcement, that 12 turrets of the kind shown in the military video below had been installed in the capital by that date. Another eight are planned.

    They are armed with a 12.7mm heavy machine gun, which is not effective against a Geran flying high and fast, but becomes effective during the final phase of its flight, when it comes within the weapon’s range. The soldier in the footage said 50 rounds were sufficient to shoot down a Geran with AI assistance.

    Details of the turrets’ precise deployment are, understandably, not yet known. However, both Russian and Ukrainian sources commented on them in interesting ways. Ukrainian expert Anatoliy Khrapchynskyi told the NV website, among other things, about the risk that fully autonomous turrets pose to civilians. Serhii Beskrestnov was the first to warn about it on Monday: “I warn you that, for your own safety, you should not stand by windows during an air-raid alert.”

    Khrapchynskyi noted that this rule has applied to any weapon since the start of the war. People should not stand by windows during air raids precisely because air defences or debris from downed weapons can damage buildings and injure people. There is a two-wall rule: if you cannot get to a shelter, hide somewhere in your flat protected from a potential blast by two walls, such as in a corridor.

    “This does not mean that robotic turrets will fire at windows. They will target moving aerial targets, but they could hit civilian infrastructure,” Khrapchynskyi conceded.

    The Russian Telegram channel Two Majors complained that while Ukraine was already using AI turrets in practice, and although promising projects of the same kind existed in Russia, bureaucracy and high costs were holding back their introduction into service.

    The same Russian source was among those that published a video showing an entire bridge across the Dnipro in Kyiv being wrapped in a counter-drone net.

    But after several days in which Russian Gerans targeted only Kyiv’s bridges, they attacked Zaporizhzhia in the same way overnight from Monday to Tuesday. Russia injured five city residents, including two Red Cross workers, and halted or restricted traffic on several bridges in Zaporizhzhia, causing traffic jams in the city during the morning.

    Zaporizhzhia lies about 30 km from the front and is a natural supply route for fighting units. Taking the bridges out of action would create a serious logistical complication, but the same applies as in Kyiv: their complete destruction is unlikely. Russia will also be satisfied with constant attacks causing minor damage, but sufficient to halt traffic.

    Among other sites hit by Russian weapons was one of the hospitals in Kryvyi Rih, which was struck by two missiles. Two people were injured during the air raid.

    Ukraine is maintaining pressure on Russia’s oil industry, reporting that it has disabled 51 percent of refinery capacity. “More than half of the enemy’s capacity has been taken out of operation. This is the result of carefully planned, methodical and systematic work aimed at exhausting Russia’s war machine and destroying its military-economic potential,” new minister Yevhen Khmara said.

    His statement cannot currently be verified, but footage of another fire at oil infrastructure in Russia emerged on Tuesday morning. It was at the Volodarskaya production and distribution centre in Moscow region. It lies just under 40 km southeast of central Moscow in a straight line, and its premises contain a large oil depot. It is also a pipeline junction through which fuel flows to Moscow, including aviation fuel for Moscow’s airports.

    Ukraine says it destroyed a Russian Su-34 and Su-35 on the ground. Satellite imagery provides no clear evidence. The attack targeted Khanskaya airfield in Krasnodar region, from which a training unit normally operates.

    The incident took place over the weekend. Satellite images showing clear traces of explosions and fire appeared relatively quickly, but it is not possible to identify what exploded and burned.

    The usual Russian source, Fighterbomber, did not comment on the matter at all.

    Russia still sees a large pocket of encircled Ukrainians in Kharkiv region, but no such pocket exists. The image below shows a map of the part of Kharkiv region where active military operations are under way. It was produced by the Russian defence ministry and shown by Two Majors on its Telegram account.

    Alongside the image, the same source again cited Kremlin claims in listing alleged Russian successes in this sector: “In the Kharkiv direction, the Northern Group of Forces reported further advances. In the Lyptsi sector, our troops advanced near Tokarivka and captured several enemy strongpoints. In the Vovchansk and Velykyi Burluk directions, advances were reported in the areas of Prykolotne, Kotivka, Varvarivka, Reznikove, Mykolaivka, and Annopil.”

    We have already written in Ukraine Battlefield update that no pocket exists, and that Ukrainian and independent sources follow the northern part of the front only marginally, because far less is happening there than Russia claims.

    Among respected OSINT projects, Playfra most recently covered this battlefield on Saturday. The first map from this source shows the section of the front located at the top right of the Russian map. This is where the alleged encirclement is supposed to be, which various Russian sources have been reporting for almost a month.

    The fighting here consists of Russian infiltration attempts, which are “chaotic and unorganised”. Playfra unequivocally rejects any encirclement.

    The following map from Playfra shows the same section of the battlefield as that seen in the Russian defence ministry’s version. The gap between reality and Russia’s claimed successes here is among the largest along the entire front, from Sumy to Kherson:

    For comparison, the same area according to Finland’s Black Bird Group:

    And according to the Russian project Slivochny Kapriz, which is relatively reliable. In all cases, Kharkiv is at the bottom left and the village of Dihtiarne, directly on the Ukrainian-Russian border, is at the top right:

    Three-quarters of Ukrainians support peace talks. In the second half of September, the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology asked respondents whether they supported peace negotiations with Russia.

    Exactly three-quarters — 75 percent — said they supported peace talks, 21 percent were against, and the remainder could not give a definite answer. This was virtually identical to the result in February 2025, when 74 percent of respondents answered the same question positively.

    This is also shown by the Kyiv polling agency’s graph, whose analysts stressed that willingness to negotiate does not equal willingness to accept Russian terms.

    Views on who will win the war have shifted more significantly. As the next graph shows, the difference between February 2025 and September 2026 is again almost zero, but there has been a significant change compared with July this year.

    At the beginning of the summer, 60 percent of Ukrainians were certain they would win the war (dark blue), while 25 percent considered it more likely than not. Now, only 47 percent are certain, but 79 percent of respondents in total still expect a Ukrainian victory.

    The change was probably driven by optimism in July, when Crimea was almost completely isolated and a successful campaign of medium-range strikes began. Although it continues, the one-off shift in public mood has since returned to its original level.

    There have been minimal changes in views on how long Ukrainians are prepared to fight. The largest group — 62 percent — said (dark blue) they were prepared to do so for as long as necessary. Four percent (light blue) said one year, while 23 percent (orange) said they could endure only a few more months. However, the number who say resistance should continue for only months has fluctuated around 20 percent for more than two years.

    Videos of the day

    Videos like this were common in 2023. It is unclear when this one was made, because the prevailing nature of the fighting is different today. The Ukrainian squad in the footage clears Russian trenches.

    In the more than seven-minute recording, views from the ground alternate with those from a reconnaissance drone hovering above the battlefield, which gave the Ukrainians an overview of the enemy. The fighting is confused, but the basic orientation is simple: Ukrainians with green identification markings attack from right to left.

    A Russian drone destroyed a balloon carrying a Ukrainian FPV drone beneath it. Ukraine is trying to use favourable wind currents in this way to extend the range of its small drones, which can then operate deeper in the Russian rear.

    Twenty-first-century warfare in Moscow. A Russian soldier with a man-portable air-defence system shot down a Ukrainian drone by firing over a busy road.

    Tethered balloons saw their greatest use during the Second World War, when they were deployed by armies on both sides. Balloon barrages protected London in the summer of 1940 and the Normandy landing fleet in June 1944, as well as German cities.

    The principle was the same as in this Russian propaganda video. Balloons tethered to the ground by cables floated above cities and militarily important targets to prevent enemy aircraft from flying low. Ideally, they would hit the cables and crash. This principle may now be applied against drones.

    A Russian FPV drone was targeting a Ukrainian unmanned ground vehicle. Just before impact, it successfully deployed a defensive launchable net.

    This was not an isolated case. Another video from a different location shows a similar situation, but this time from the perspective of a camera on the ground drone.

    What are the losses

    No update on Tuesday.

    • By Monday (5 October), Russia had verifiably lost 24,170 pieces of heavy equipment (24,138 on Tuesday, 22 September). Of these, Ukraine destroyed 19,133 (19,105), 1,003 (1,000) were damaged, crews abandoned 1,194 (1,194), and the Ukrainian army captured 2,840 (2,839). This includes 4,452 (4,448) tanks, of which 3,357 (3,353) were destroyed in combat.
    • Ukraine lost 12,238 (12,175) pieces of equipment, of which 9,633 (9,579) were destroyed, 711 (702) damaged, 695 (695) abandoned and 1,199 (1,199) captured. This includes 1,466 (1,464) tanks, of which 1,126 (1,125) were destroyed in combat.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its fatalities or destroyed equipment. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. This overview uses data from the Oryx project, which has compiled a list of equipment losses documented exclusively by photographs since the beginning of the war.

    ]]>         Centre-right’s Muslim Brotherhood witch-hunt in EU Parliament risks criminalising everyday activism https://euobserver.com/241087/centre-rights-muslim-brotherhood-witch-hunt-in-eu-parliament-risks-criminalising-everyday-activism/ Tue, 06 Oct 2026 09:06:48 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241087 If Brussels accepts this vague hunt for “Muslim Brotherhood networks”, the same logic could later be turned against almost any vocal minority in Europe.]]> On Wednesday (7 October), the largest group in the European Parliament, the European People’s Party (EPP), has scheduled a debate on a “European Parliament resolution on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network.”

    The move follows the adoption of an EPP party resolution that treats Muslim civic engagement as inherently suspect and collective religious practice as a potential threat.

    It largely mirrored the German Christian Democratic approach of criminalising Muslim civic engagement.

    As Brussels-based EU expert and EUobserver’s columnist Shada Islam put it, the supposed fight against “political Islam” “places Muslim political and civic activity inside an almost exclusively security framework,” and thus “European democracy is hollowed out rather than reinforced when an entire religious or ethnic minority and its civil society are regarded as permanently suspect.”

    Also, the resolution protects religious freedom for Muslims only as an individual right, explicitly stating that it seeks to ensure “equality among citizens, rather than collective claims,” leaving the collective expression of Islam unprotected and thus hollowing out the very idea of religious freedom.

    As also the to be debated motion shows, it is unclear where protected religious activity ends and dangerous political activity begins.

    Islamophobic conspiracies

    The notion of “Islamist entryism,” imported from France, has become a way to criminalise Muslim participation in civil society and politics.

    The resolution describes it as “a political strategy of influence, progressive structuring, institutional penetration and ideological legitimisation,” which it separates from the “peaceful practice of Islam.”

    But how does one tell the “good” Muslims, who engage peacefully in politics and lobby policymakers to stand up for their rights, from the bad? Or is the good Muslim simply the apolitical one, who does not stand up for the protection of their collective human rights?

    Read more

    Europe’s dangerous art of anti-Muslim doublespeak

    If “political Islam” is a problem because it is described “as a societal project,” how does it differ from the collective efforts of Jews, Christians, and others, who also “produce collective norms,” as the motion puts it?

    And if “Islamist influence operates through a broad and fragmented ecosystem of associations, foundations, cultural, educational, religious, charitable, university, youth, anti-discrimination or social action structures,” something equally true of Christian, Jewish, and other religious groups, then where does the EPP draw the line between peaceful Muslim activity and Islamist activity that has to be banned?

    Isn’t the claim that Muslim “community allegiances placed above common law” a typical Islamophobic allegation, familiar from the old mistrust of Jews as more loyal to a global Jewish community than to the nation-state?

    Is this the old antisemitism in new “Muslim” clothes?

    Indeed, the motion lists a catalogue of anti-Muslim conspiracy theories: “separatist narratives, systematic victimhood, antisemitism, hatred of Israel, conspiracy narratives, challenges to secularism … may constitute markers of ideological radicalisation or Islamist influence.” They may. And what if they don’t?

    Read more

    Far-right prejudice now ‘normalised’ across Europe, warns EU anti-racism chief 

    Guilty until proven innocent

    What follows seems to be one of the motion’s primary goals: cutting funds for Muslim and anti-racist civil society organizations such as the Forum of European Muslim Youth and Student Organisations (FEMYSO) and the European Network Against Racism (ENAR), who are both registered in the EU transparency register of Belgium and annually audited.

    These CSOs are seen as a manifestation of political Islam per se even though they have denied any those connections.

    And it is a form of innocence that cannot easily be proven.

    The EPP motion claims that “some Islamist networks are able … to adopt the vocabulary of fundamental rights, inclusion, diversity, intercultural dialogue, anti-racism and the fight against discrimination, while promoting in other spaces logics of separation, community pressure or contestation of democratic principles.” In other words, the better integrated Muslims in Europe are, the more suspicious they may become.

    Shaky legal foundations

    The EPP’s motion builds on highly problematic bills, legislation and political procedures. It quotes the French ministry of the interior’s 2025 report “Muslim Brotherhood and political Islamism in France,” which has been harshly criticised.

    It also cites a resolution of the French National Assembly from January 2026 that urged the European Union to add the Muslim Brotherhood to its list of terrorist organisations and to lobby for it.

    The resolution was voted against by 101 members of parliament, some of whom called it “Islamophobic.” The motion also invokes the contested Austrian Symbols Act, which prohibits the symbols of non-violent organisations that are not considered illegal under domestic legislation and lumps them together with those of jihadist groups ISIS and Al-Qaeda.

    A further cited motion is from the Dutch parliament in March 2026 and calls for a ban on the Muslim Brotherhood and linked organisations, but it too has no legislative relevance so far.

    None of these motions or laws has outlawed “Islamist entryism” or the “Muslim Brotherhood networks.”

    Yet the EPP resolution builds on exactly this shaky ground while pretending that its own motion is solid.

    More importantly, the way Austria and France treat their Muslims is well documented: from the infamous, massive and racist police raids known as Operation Luxor to the French state’s Systemic Obstruction policy, which resulted in 101 government units nationwide monitoring Islam and Muslims, 24,887 Muslim organizations and businesses placed on a secret blacklist and under strict monitoring, and the closure of 718 Muslim-owned organizations and businesses, with €46m seized. There is nothing here that should be emulated elsewhere.

    Read more

    Why Europe’s anti-racism strategy fails to deliver

    Crude logic

    The EPP’s argument that “Hamas on the EU list of terrorist organisations historically originates from the Muslim Brotherhood movement” rests on crude logic.

    Both the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats (S&D) and the secular Marxist-Leninist Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), similarly considered a “terrorist organization,” have Marxist origins. Outlaw the S&D as a consequence?

    Today, it is Muslims who are being surveilled, monitored and criminalised. Who is it tomorrow? If this resolution passes, life for politically conscious Muslims who are defending their right to exist in Europe will become even more difficult. And tomorrow potentially everybody’s life.

    Until now, German chancellor Friedrich Merz had been reluctant to bring the nuclear topic on the table, partly because there was no agreement within his coalition. He has even said that Germany’s nuclear phase-out was irreversible. But that position is not shared by everyone in his own party.

    And as support for the far-right AfD (Alternative for Germany) grows — a party that is strongly in favour of nuclear power — nuclear energy is becoming less politically taboo in Germany.

    According to a non-public document sent by Berlin to other EU member states and reported by the media Euractiv (currently Rapporteur), the German government wants nuclear energy to be taken into account when the EU sets its climate targets for 2040.

    The logic is similar to the debate over the EU’s 2035 target for new cars: the overall objective remains, but countries could have more flexibility over how they achieve it.

    And that proposal is likely to be welcomed in France. But could they convince a majority of EU countries? The picture across Europe is changing.

    Many EU countries already operate nuclear power plants, while others are building new reactors or considering a return to nuclear. Italy, for example, is looking to revive a nuclear industry after abandoning nuclear power following the 1986 Chernobyl disaster.

    Poland has never operated a nuclear power plant, but it is now developing its first one. And several other countries that currently have no reactors are seriously considering building them.

    Slovakia was ultimately represented by Marek Eštok, state secretary at the foreign ministry.

    Andrej Babiš’s Czech government all but completely ignored the initiative. As Respekt magazine wrote, Babiš declined the opportunity to visit Ukraine and did not send any representative to Bukovel.

    So Czechia was represented at the summit only by opposition deputy Senate president Jiří Drahoš.

    And Austria was ultimately represented by Christine Schwarz-Fuchs, president of the Federal Council.

    Hungary sent Ádám Ceglédi, the acting chargé d’affaires at the Hungarian embassy in Kyiv, as the Hungarian foreign ministry confirmed to Telex.

    Ukraine expected stronger support

    “There are many different forms of cooperation in this region: the Visegrád Four, the Slavkov format and the Central European Initiative. Ukraine is interested in improving its relations with some countries,” Péter Techet, a foreign-policy analyst and researcher at the Institute for Danube Region and Central Europe in Vienna, said.

    According to the analyst, Ukraine may have hoped that Orbán’s fall would bring a clear shift in Hungary’s Ukraine policy. Anita Orbán, as foreign minister, has confirmed this by pursuing a foreign policy moving away from Russia.

    However, Ukrainians did not take Magyar’s domestic political interests into account.

    Read more

    EU moves to unlock €4.2bn for Hungary as Magyar strengthens rule-of-law and corruption rules

    Magyar panders to anti-Ukraine crowd

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/06/scottish-islanders-highest-level-diesel-prices-uk-hebrides-shetland</link>
      <description><p>Inhabitants of the Hebrides and Shetland tell of how fuel costs are putting the squeeze on commuting, services, food and more</p><p>As fuel prices reach the highest level in the UK since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Scottish islanders are feeling the pain more than most. On the mainland, the price of diesel has soared to a record high of 200.01p a litre, bringing the cost of filling an average family car to more than £110, according to the RAC. Petrol has risen by a third since the start of the Iran war at the end of February, averaging 174.71p – increasing to 195.64p in motorway service areas.</p><p>In the Hebrides and Shetland, prices at the forecourt have jumped even higher, with some fuel stations selling diesel for more than 220p a litre during the initial rise.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/06/scottish-islanders-highest-level-diesel-prices-uk-hebrides-shetland">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Virgin Media O2 complains of ‘stitch-up’ over rival provider, which has 1.5m customers</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/nils-pratley-on-finance/2026/oct/05/bt-purchase-talktalk-politically-sensible">Nils Pratley: BT’s purchase of TalkTalk is cosy – but probably politically sensible</a></p></li></ul><p>BT has agreed to buy the broadband supplier TalkTalk out of administration in a £400m rescue deal that will save 900 jobs.</p><p>The company said it had struck a deal to acquire TalkTalk and its wholesale business PlatformX Communications (PXC) on a debt-free basis, in a move that is expected to cost it £400m.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/05/bt-buy-broadband-supplier-talktalk-jobs">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>BT’s purchase of TalkTalk is cosy – but probably politically sensible | Nils Pratley</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/nils-pratley-on-finance/2026/oct/05/bt-purchase-talktalk-politically-sensible</link>
      <description><p>For all the howls of a ‘stitch-up’, it’s hard to see what ministers were supposed to do, as the alternatives risked worse outcomes</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/05/bt-buy-broadband-supplier-talktalk-jobs">BT to buy broadband supplier TalkTalk in £400m rescue deal, saving 900 jobs</a></p></li></ul><p>“All the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest,” thundered Virgin Media O2. It’s not an unreasonable view of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/05/bt-buy-broadband-supplier-talktalk-jobs">BT’s hurried weekend acquisition of TalkTalk</a>. Once upon a time, TalkTalk was seen as a plucky upstart performing the useful role of irritant to BT’s giant Openreach broadband operation. Now the challenger is being consumed by the dominant player via a pre-pack administration that minimises short-term political headaches.</p><p>Here’s the problem, though, with the cosy stitch-up thesis. For all the howls of outrage, it’s hard to see what the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, who gave her blessing by issuing a little-used public interest notice, was supposed to do differently. Alternative approaches, notably a chaotic collapse of TalkTalk without a rescue plan for the customers, risked worse outcomes.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/nils-pratley-on-finance/2026/oct/05/bt-purchase-talktalk-politically-sensible">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess | Gaby Hinsliff</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/06/andy-burnham-eu-tories-kemi-badenoch-brexit</link>
      <description><p>Badenoch would never have reopened the door on Brexit, but now that the PM has, it suits the Conservatives to let him walk through it</p><p>There’s no way on earth it should have worked, but somehow he may have got away with it. Last week, the actor <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/news/video/2026/oct/02/celebrity-traitors-has-richard-e-grant-blown-it-already-the-latest">Richard E Grant</a> became the first contestant on The Traitors – a show whose only unbreakable rule is never to let anyone know you’re the murderer – to gleefully announce within minutes of being selected that yes, haha, <em>it’s him!</em> Yet even then many of his fellow contestants seemed to like him too much to recoil.</p><p>And that, roughly speaking, is now Andy Burnham’s Brexit strategy. After years of Labour politicians – not least Burnham himself, <a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx21en4807wo">in the Makerfield byelection</a>, without which he would not now be prime minister – trying to hide their real feelings about Brexit, Burnham has decided just to tell the truth and hope people roll with it. Leaving hasn’t worked, he said bluntly <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/sep/30/andy-burnham-uk-could-go-all-the-way-rejoining-eu">last week in Liverpool</a>, and Britain should consider the alternatives. If you’re a leaver who suspects him of being out to unwind Brexit – well, yes, he is. This bold strategy seemingly surprised <a href="https://observer.co.uk/news/politics/article/nobody-was-expecting-this-burnham-u-turn-on-road-back-to-europe-leaves-whitehall-reeling">much of his own cabinet</a>, an early lesson in how he likes to work for those who hadn’t studied his Manchester operation closely enough. But the oddly muted initial response to what would once have been a seismic shock suggests it’s wrongfooting some opponents, too.</p><p>Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/06/andy-burnham-eu-tories-kemi-badenoch-brexit">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>The Guardian view on Tory economics: Britain’s future needs more than Thatcher’s past | Editorial</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/05/the-guardian-view-on-tory-economics-britains-future-needs-more-than-thatchers-past</link>
      <description><p>The Conservatives blame their failures on abandoning their 1976 principles. But the country needs investment and resilience rather than another round of spending cuts</p><p>The Conservative party wants to go back to the future under Kemi Badenoch. In her foundational text, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/oct/04/for-kemi-being-the-nasty-party-is-not-toxic-but-a-badge-of-honour">The Right Way</a>, released at the weekend, the Tory party leader makes its intellectual lineage explicit, repeatedly invoking Margaret Thatcher’s <a href="https://www.margaretthatcher.org/document/109439">1976 policy statement The Right Approach</a>. The 2026 economic framework is familiar: only private enterprise creates wealth; taxes, regulation and spending can obstruct growth and competition; markets make the country stronger. The speech by her shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, made it clear that Conservative failures over its 14-year spell in charge were the result of the party straying from Thatcherite principles.</p><p>One might argue that, on the contrary, errors were because the party slavishly followed such a creed. When Rough, a depleted North Sea gasfield that once provided around 70% of the UK’s gas-storage capacity, was judged uneconomic by its private owner, a Conservative government in 2017 accepted that international markets could provide the UK with adequate energy security. That proved to be a big mistake when Russia invaded Ukraine, sending fossil fuel prices upwards. Britain was particularly exposed as a net energy importer and highly dependent on gas. Tory ministers had to bring back Rough into operation in 2022. Mrs Badenoch puts its closure down to “<a href="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6760307b23436bea5cfc749e/6abe82ddb8322e0cfd6d31e5_f62154aa693cdddcbbac38806b158324_The%20Right%20Way.pdf">false&nbsp;economies</a>”. But what was wrong was putting private profitability ahead of the country’s needs.</p><p><em><strong>Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/tone/letters"> letters</a> section, please <a href="mailto:guardian.letters@theguardian.com?body=Please%20include%20your%20name,%20full%20postal%20address%20and%20phone%20number%20with%20your%20letter%20below.%20Letters%20are%20usually%20published%20with%20the%20author%27s%20name%20and%20city/town/village.%20The%20rest%20of%20the%20information%20is%20for%20verification%20only%20and%20to%20contact%20you%20where%20necessary.">click here</a>.</strong></em></p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/05/the-guardian-view-on-tory-economics-britains-future-needs-more-than-thatchers-past">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Our ‘genius’ president is revealing his ignorance of economics, fueling concerns about the threat he poses to the world</p><p>Donald Trump recently made a bold claim about his abilities, <a href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117269745153543631">writing on Truth Social</a>: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”</p><p>But in the days before and after that post, Trump made one mind-boggling statement after another, including one that <a href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117213056648777213">raised the possibility of cutting off all trade</a> with dozens of the US’s trading partners. The president’s statements had many experts questioning not just his intelligence, but also whether he – and the outlandish policies he was proposing – were a clear and present danger to both the US economy and the world economy. Public respect for Trump’s economic sense has fallen so low that just 7% of Americans think he should take the lead in regulating AI, according to <a href="https://prod-i.a.dj.com/public/resources/documents/Redacted_WSJ_Poll_Sept_2026.pdf">a recent WSJ poll</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/05/trump-us-economy-comments">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Preppers used to be ridiculed – but we’re all stockpiling now | Zoe Williams</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/05/preppers-used-to-be-ridiculed-but-were-all-stockpiling-now</link>
      <description><p>The UK government urging households to prepare for unknown threats with a three-day supply of food and water doesn’t feel like an overreaction. But is there a bigger plan to go with it?</p><p>There is no national food stockpile and there hasn’t been since it was wound up in the 1990s. It feels like a metaphor for the delusions of that era: nothing bad can possibly happen again; no two countries with a McDonald’s have gone to war with each other (according to the journalist Thomas L Friedman, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1996/12/08/opinion/foreign-affairs-big-mac-i.html?eafs_enabled=false">also in the 90s</a>). Now, we all have a McDonald’s and wars regularly disrupt food supplies. The problem with metaphors is you can’t eat them – not even satisfying ones.<strong> </strong></p><p>For people who remember the second world war, or feel as if they do, there is always enough muscle memory to do topical household stockpiling. My mum kept a trunk of food that was mainly filled with condensed milk in case of a nuclear war, all the way through the 80s. When the Berlin Wall came down, we should have had a ceremonial toffee-sauce-making event where we ate it all, but we didn’t; in 1990, she was stockpiling again, to mark the Gulf war.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/05/preppers-used-to-be-ridiculed-but-were-all-stockpiling-now">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/05/british-government-food-national-security-crisis-shortages</link>
      <description><p>Experts say country does not have plan to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for future shortages</p><p>Britain does not have a plan for how to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for potential future food shortages, according to a warning from more than 150 experts delivered to Andy Burnham.</p><p>The climate crisis, geopolitical shocks, cyber-attacks and energy outages are among the threats to food chain security, according to the open letter, which claims the government is “complacent about food as a national security matter”.</p><p>Establish a new system of local food resilience committees under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004.</p><p>Audit the UK’s reliance on a few very large food companies and food imports.</p><p>Realign national food production around nutritional needs.</p><p>Create national, regional, local and community food storage schemes.</p><p>Support the decentralisation of the UK’s food supply.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/05/british-government-food-national-security-crisis-shortages">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/06/the-butter-boom-how-the-world-fell-back-in-love-with-the-glorious-golden-spread</link>
      <description><p>It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff?</p><p>Temperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.”</p><p>I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/06/the-butter-boom-how-the-world-fell-back-in-love-with-the-glorious-golden-spread">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>A story of storico ribelle, produced by a small group of mountain herders according to a traditional farming system based on seasonal and rotational grazing</p><p>My journey into the world of storico ribelle began with a shared passion for photography and the mountains. A close friend of mine lives in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/2023/jun/16/travelling-to-pastures-old-in-the-orobie-alps-a-photo-essay">Orobie Alps</a>. He loves the mountains and the natural environment that surrounds him, and we share the same passion for photography. When I finally went to visit him, I discovered a way of experiencing the mountains that was very different from the one I knew growing up in the Apennines, where I come from.</p><p>What struck me was not only the landscape, but the relationship people still have with it. Here, I discovered a world where the mountain is not simply a place to visit or explore, but a place to live and work. A world where cheese is still a tradition rather than an industrial product, and where the rhythms of the seasons, the animals and the daily work of the <em>alpeggiatori</em> – the mountain herders – are still deeply connected.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/ng-interactive/2026/oct/05/rebel-cheesemakers-alpine-tradition-storico-ribelle">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/oct/03/london-mansions-sell-house-prices-prime-property</link>
      <description><p>For decades, the capital’s house prices raced ahead of the national average – but now they are falling in prime areas</p><p>An elegant Georgian facade, a full-width balcony and an exclusive address in South Kensington just steps from the Natural History Museum and the V&amp;A. Yet the listing price of this <a href="https://sothebysrealty.co.uk/properties/buy/flat-for-sale-london-south-kensington-queens-gate-gardens-45029/">west London flat</a> at Queen’s Gate Gardens has dropped by nearly £1m since last year, to £4.4m.</p><p>It is far from an isolated case. A nearby house originally listed at £20m was slashed to £14m this year, says a local estate agent. In neighbouring Notting Hill, a stucco-fronted property that came to market two years ago at £16m is now being offered for less than £14m, they said.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/oct/03/london-mansions-sell-house-prices-prime-property">Continue reading...</a></description>
