In a subsequent justification for the ruling, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily, judge Konrad Mielcarek wrote that Romanowski had pledged to “voluntarily return to the country”.

Conditions for his safe passage include Romanowski reporting to the court and prosecutors at designated times and places, not leaving his declared place of residence, and not seeking to obstruct the criminal proceedings against him.

The judge said that prosecutors had failed to provide adequate arguments as to why Romanowski’s request should be denied. He also found that Romanowski had not obstructed proceedings against him, but had merely exercised available legal remedies.

The fact that Romanowski had fled Poland does not count against him, argued the judge. In fact, “the very nature of safe passage is to provide a person residing abroad with a legal guarantee…in exchange for voluntarily submitting to the jurisdiction of Polish authorities”.

The judge also clarified that safe passage is neither a “reward” nor a “privilege” and that, given that evidence in the case is already secured and Romanowski no longer has influence over justice ministry officials, the risk of tampering is low.

 

The National Prosecutor’s Office immediately issued a statement declaring its opposition to the ruling and its intention to appeal. It noted that there had been no confirmation that Romanowski really is in Tiraspol and that the suspect had repeatedly sought to evade the law.

Żurek, meanwhile, noted that Mielcarek is one of the so-called “neo-judges”, appointed by a judicial body rendered illegitimate by PiS’s reforms. There are legal doubts about the status of such judges and the rulings issued by them, some of which have been overturned on that basis.

In his statement, the justice minister also argued that, under the law, safe passage cannot be issued without a prosecutor’s consent. Lewandowski, however, cited examples of case law that he said disproved this. He also noted that prosecutors had not filed any motion to recuse Mielcarek from the case.

Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? | ★★★★☆ | @sohoplace

Edward Albee’s Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? is one of those plays that only seems to come around every decade or so – and when it does you wonder where it’s been all this time. It’s lost none of its caustic charm over the six decades since it was first performed, its depiction of married life as bleak and devastating as ever.

Last time this play was in the West End, the wonderful Imelda Staunton played Martha. This time it’s a very different beast: Gillian Anderson puts in a lithe, exaggeratedly sexual performance as the daughter of a prestigious college president, with renowned character actor Billy Crudup playing her professor husband George.

It opens with George and Martha bickering after a night out. They’re both good and drunk and thirsty for more. Fortunately, Martha has invited company: an ambitious young lecturer and his wife. 

The initial thrill of seeing Anderson and Crudup is soon eroded by the creeping sense of dread brought on by the psychic damage each seems intent on inflicting upon the other. Like Hedda Gabler or Revolutionary Road, this is one of those texts to avoid should you be experiencing relationship troubles. Albee dissects his characters with the precision of a surgeon, albeit one with a sadistic streak. Martha is a belligerent drunk, revelling in belittling her husband and his floundering career. George in turn belittles the prickly upstart Nick, for whom he makes no attempt to mask his contempt. Nobody is enjoying this rotten night in but at least the alcohol flows as freely as the bile.

Gillian Anderson is superb

Anderson is predictably superb as Martha, a magnetic presence despite the sharpness of her tongue. But it’s Crudup’s performance you’ll be thinking of on the journey home. Quieter and more reserved than his wife, there’s a simmering menace to his George. While Martha is quick to throw insults, George quietly dismantles the defences of his guests before neatly skewering them one after another. 

The staging is fantastically chic, taking full advantage of Soho Place’s in-the-round configuration. The audience is positioned around a circular 1960s mid-century modern living room; there’s something gladiatorial about the set-up, the crowd sitting on the front row for this monumental scrap. You may not get splattered by literal blood from this contest but you might catch a stray gin if you’re not careful.

Just don’t expect an early knock-out: this is a long, long night’s journey into the day. It’s well over three hours, including two intervals, although for the second you’re not allowed to leave your seat (which is all the more torturous for those of us with full bladders). When the end comes, it’s with a sense of relief – both that the fighting is finally over and that you can quickly escape to the bathroom.

• Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf starring Gillian Anderson is on now at @sohoplace

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has launched a probe into how the regulatory body interacted with a whistleblower who recently took his own life.

Simon Andriesz, a former managing director at BGC Partners, had blown the whistle on alleged links between the US secretary of commerce Howard Lutnick and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. He died last week after taking his own life at 57 years old.

In response, the Transparency Task Force, of which Andriesz was a member, has called for an inquiry into the FCA’s handling of whistleblowers, with John McDonnell MP, chair of the all-party parliamentary group on investment fraud and fairer financial services, leading the call.

The campaign group said the FCA had advised Andriesz that he had lost whistleblower protection because his identity had become known, which was incorrect, and that the FCA apologised and said it would provide further guidance and training to its whistleblowing team.

The group also highlighted that Andriesz had raised concerns over the “poor treatment of whistleblowers by the FCA” which led him to appeal to senior executives of the watchdog for help when he believed the retaliation against him was escalating and when he and his family were in crisis.

On the call for the inquiry, McDonnell said: “We are aware that research into the FCA’s handling of whistleblowers was carried out in 2021/2022, but
that time the FCA were allowed to ‘mark their own homework’.”

“Concerns have been raised about the suspiciously small sample size they used and even whether the FCA may have selected whom to survey,” he added.

FCA board member to lead review

In direct response to mounting pressure after Andriesz’s death, the FCA asked independent board member Lea Paterson to examine whether the FCA failed in its duty of care toward a vulnerable individual who took significant personal risks to report alleged wrongdoing.

In a press statement on Tuesday, Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA’s general counsel, said the watchdog “shared our condolences, and our thoughts are with his family and loved ones”.

He said: “To build greater confidence, we’re sharing more information with whistleblowers about the action we take. We provided feedback on each of the 1,252 whistleblowing reports we closed last year.

“We know, though, frustrations remain. Legal restrictions can mean we’re not able to share as much as people understandably want, and sometimes the actions we take don’t meet people’s expectations.

“We must be open and consider if there are ways in which we can improve, especially in how we interact with people who may be particularly vulnerable. I’m grateful to Lea [Paterson] for taking on this important work. We plan to share any lessons she thinks we should learn from, and how we’ll take them forward, early next year,” he added.

The FCA was cleared of wrongdoing in 2024 after an investigation into his handling of a whistleblower complaint. In the same year, the watchdog said it will look to strengthen its internal whistleblowing policy after intense criticism over its handling of complaints from former staff.

Policymakers should do more to protect vulnerable households from surges in inflation caused by geopolitical events like the Iran war, the IMF says in a newly-published chapter of its world economic outlook that looks set to spark further debate about the UK’s welfare bill.

The IMF’s intervention comes as the conflict in the Middle East threatens to derail John Healey’s Budget next month, as energy prices and global borrowing costs surge. 

Researchers at consultancy EY have warned that the Iran war has already narrowed the Chancellor’s fiscal headroom to £11bn and could wipe it out entirely if the conflict rages on.

But the IMF has encouraged governments to commit to spending to protect their most vulnerable citizens from the cost-of-living shocks caused by events like the Middle East conflict and the Ukraine war. 

Policymakers should pay better attention to the long-lasting effects that temporary geopolitical shocks can have on low-income households, the organisation said. 

The IMF has urged governments and central banks to look at targeted and temporary support measures as “the most effective and cost-efficient way to protect poorer households when prices for the basics spike”. 

UK ‘skating on thin ice’

UK inflation inched up from 2.9 to 3.1 per cent in August and industry figures have warned that food inflation is set to surge above six per cent by next summer.

“Assistance, when warranted, should be temporary and delivered primarily through income-support measures directed at the most vulnerable households, ideally using existing social protection systems that can be scaled up rapidly,” the IMF said.

Its world economic outlook instructs policymakers to prioritise targeted measures over broad-brush interventions like tax cuts, price caps and subsidies. 

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to deliver “breathing space” to households struggling with the cost of living. He has cut VAT on energy bills and capped bus fares at £2. 

But economists have warned that soaring borrowing costs and sky-high government borrowing means the government will have its hands tied at the Budget next month. 

Andy Haldane, a former Bank of England chief economist, said on Tuesday that the government is fiscally “skating on pretty thin ice” as he warned against further tax rises.

Haldane, who was an informal adviser to Burnham but refused a formal role in his government, told CNBC that the “single most effective way” for Labour to gain fiscal credibility would be to “show that it’s able and willing to take the knife to public spending.

]]> 2463422Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Robert De Niro on $1.3billion hospitality empire: ‘I’m very protective of Nobu’ https://www.cityam.com/robert-de-niro-movies-are-different-nobu-im-very-protective-of/ Tue, 06 Oct 2026 12:39:37 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2462164

Goodfellas and Taxi Driver legend Robert De Niro talks exclusively to City AM The Magazine about his hospitality empire, which quietly occupies the 83-year-old New York-born actor in-between his film-making. Over the last 40 years, De Niro has been launching Nobu restaurants around the world, a Japanese brand he is fiercely protective of. He speaks [...]]]>

Goodfellas and Taxi Driver legend Robert De Niro talks exclusively to City AM The Magazine about his hospitality empire, which quietly occupies the 83-year-old New York-born actor in-between his film-making. Over the last 40 years, De Niro has been launching Nobu restaurants around the world, a Japanese brand he is fiercely protective of. He speaks to us about maintaining the quality at all costs, how restaurant work differs from the movies, and the concept of ‘ikigai’, which means never retiring

In an intimidatingly futuristic building made almost entirely of glass, I pass through a marble-clad lobby, up a flight of stairs and into an expensive-looking hotel suite. Here a handful of serious-looking people sit around a brightly lit boardroom table. Most of them are hospitality professionals: a general manager, a chief executive, a gaggle of publicists. One of them is the most famous actor in the world.

Robert De Niro looks at the ground, channelling all of his energy into standing up to shake my hand. He lifts slowly out of his chair but I ask him to, please, sit down, don’t get up on my account. He’s shrunk a little from his heyday, his shoulders more rounded, but that’s all that reveals his 83 years. And if he’s a little less formidable, it’s only physically. His vibe is still deadly: De Niro would rather spit than say a single word more than is necessary, or, worse, a word he didn’t mean.

Robert De Niro and the Nobu story

We’re at Nobu Portman Square hotel in Marylebone, part of the group the actor co-founded in the 1990s, a fact that still carries a sheen of unbelievability even after three decades. De Niro isn’t even the only octogenarian around this table. Also joining us is Nobu co-founder Meir Teper, the 83-year-old film producer who, like De Niro, side-hustles as a lifestyle tycoon.

De Niro is here to discuss the three Nobu Hotel & Residences opening in Egypt, including a restaurant on the north coast that’s already started plating up sushi, and the phased launches over the next five years of resorts in Cairo and the coastline. Residences are also soon-to-launch in Manchester, as is Nobu’s first wellness club and countryside retreat, Nobu Woolfox, which will open next year on an estate near Rutland in the Midlands, rivalling luxury offerings in the Cotswolds. De Niro is coming for the wellness industry, too.

Nobu is an incredible success story. There are now 19 Nobu hotels and 55 restaurants serving namesake chef Nobu Matsuhisa’s Japanese-Peruvian cuisine. International openings are green-lit by De Niro himself, who is a kind of vibe checker for the brand. As Teper puts it: “We follow his vision.” The story goes that De Niro convinced chef Nobu to open a restaurant in Tribeca in New York in 1994; that flagship, still thriving, was the beginning of a global empire now estimated to be worth $1.3 billion (De Niro, Teper and Matsuhisa are understood to own 80 per cent; with the other 20 per cent held by private equity firm Blackstone).

He’ll say, ‘I don’t think we belong here’

By all accounts, De Niro has an instinct for destinations that will – and crucially, will not – work. Sometimes that instinct seems to border on the preternatural: when our sister publication spoke to him in 2025, he admitted he’d never been to Manchester and knew nothing about the city, despite having commissioned a Nobu Residences there. So how on earth does a man regarded as one of the best actors of his generation know what makes a good location for a Japanese restaurant? “I just say, ‘Where do I wanna go?’” De Niro tells me. He really does speak in that smash-em-up, gravelly, menacing tone. “Would I like to walk into that restaurant in that particular place?” He scrunches his face to make an impression of a first-time visitor. “That first sight, where it is, what part of the world… it’s important.”

His strategy clearly works: only five Nobu restaurants have closed in 30 years, which is especially impressive when you consider the hardships faced by the hospitality industry (in London alone half of restaurants shut within two years of their first service). Madonna once said you could tell if a city was going to be fun by whether it had a Nobu in it. In keeping with De Niro’s reputation for speaking his mind, he’ll happily draw a red line through potential new locations. “He’ll say: ‘I don’t think we belong here,’” says Teper. “I don’t want to name names, but it’s not like when somebody approaches us we just say ‘Okay let’s do it.’”

De Niro inspired by eating on location

When I ask De Niro what’s unique about the brand, he says it’s simple: the quality of the food and the location. There is no pandering to trends, no evolving ‘concept’. It’s just good sushi. It was British film director Roland Joffé who first introduced De Niro to the cooking of Nobu Matsuhisa in the late 1980s and it was love at first bite. At that point, chef Nobu had only one restaurant in Los Angeles. “Roland said, ‘Come to this restaurant, you’ll like it,’” remembers De Niro. “I was maybe an hour into eating and meeting Nobu and I said ‘If you ever want to open a restaurant in New York just let me know.’

“For me it was a no-brainer. It would work in New York. And here [in London], too. The Japanese restaurants I’d been to were all the same. Very good, but conservative, staid, nothing exciting. They didn’t pretend to be. But Nobu had another thing, the Latin from his time in Peru, that made it special. So that was it: I said: ‘This will work’. I’d opened a grill with Drew Nieporent, a local restaurateur in Tribeca, a year or two before I met Nobu and I put him and Drew together. It took a while to get it going, Nobu was apprehensive. I can’t remember all the details but finally it happened.”

The question is, why?

The partnership makes sense. While Nobu, 76, was brought up slicing fish and thinking about flavour, De Niro spent years travelling the world filming, developing an eagle eye for what makes a restaurant people want to hang out in.

The bigger question, though, is… why? Why does one of the most lauded actors in the world spend his time promoting expensive condos in Egypt when he’s already worth an estimated $500m? Especially when he might not even live to see them completed? And how does an 83-year-old factor business into his life when he has a three-year-old daughter, who in a recent interview, through tears, he described as the “pure joy” in his life? “She has a very sweet kind of way of looking at you,” De Niro told AARP. “And just taking you in… They just look at you and take it in. I want to be around for as long as I can, to enjoy it, to enjoy her.” He lives with his girlfriend, 46-year-old martial arts instructor and dancer Tiffany Chen, and his youngest daughter in a 100 acre Hudson Valley property that boasts its own ski slope. He has seven children altogether with four women; the oldest, Drena, is 55.

Maintain the quality. Period. It’s that simple.

I suggest it’s unusual for someone of his age to be working at all, let alone as the co-founder of an international hospitality empire. De Niro nods deeply and puts up no defence. Does he find something here he can’t in Hollywood? Like, is the public-facing world of film sets and red carpets passé compared to the rigour of the luxury restaurant world? Just for a second, I experience old-school De Niro: He tenses his facial muscles to pull that characteristically strained expression, as if he’s just sucked on a lemon. “No, that’s different,” he says, in combat mode. “It’s just a different thing. I enjoy it and feel very protective of it because I’m part of the creative… We all want to make sure we maintain the quality and everything. That’s it. That’s the key. You’ve got to be careful with that stuff.”

What happens if the quality isn’t maintained? “We were talking about this the other day – someone was saying, ‘Why have you got to spend that?’. But somebody will visit and notice that’s something a little… off. And then maybe they notice something else and then something else, and all of a sudden it’s not the same restaurant. Then people start to say, ‘Nah I don’t wanna go there.’ The only thing you can do is maintain the quality. Period. It’s that simple.”

Nobu offers a sense of control

His acting roles have, of course, changed with age: he’s unlikely to play a character as iconic as Travis Bickle today. Perhaps the Nobu empire offers De Niro a sense of control, speculates PR guru Mark Borkowski, who has worked with Michael Jackson, Prince and Macaulay Culkin. “The parts inevitably narrow: patriarch, mob elder, grandfather. Nobu reverses the power relationship,” he says. “Here, De Niro says ‘Yes’. He chooses where to appear, when to appear and what bears his name. The business makes acting optional, and perhaps at his age optional is the only kind of work worth doing. In a curious way, it is still the same job he has always done: turn up somewhere beautifully lit, hit the mark, say very little and allow everyone else to project meaning onto him. The difference is that now he owns a piece of the room.”

Nobu has undoubtedly had a good run, but it isn’t what it once was. In the noughties, the Park Lane restaurant – the second in the world to open after Tribeca – was a celeb magnet, the number one destination for actors on the junket circuit. It’s part of the same building that housed the Met Bar, once the city’s coolest watering hole; 20 years ago, that 50 metre stretch of real estate was the most coveted in London. But the creatives have moved on: now the majority of the visitors to Nobu’s London restaurants appear to be international.

Robert De Niro: movies not to miss

Today the brand is courted not by the coolest cities in the world, but the ones that wish to replicate the aura of the coolest cities in the world. It is a brand synonymous with ‘placemaking’, helping to establish burgeoning destinations like the Egyptian coast that are keen to welcome moneyed Western visitors. “People are constantly asking us to be in their place to give them a certain cachet or credibility,” De Niro says in a press conference following our interview.

You could, at a stretch, liken the trajectory of Nobu to De Niro’s film career. He was an unstoppable heavyweight during the 1980s and 1990s, when his collaborations with Martin Scorsese on Goodfellas, Taxi Driver, Raging Bull and Casino made him the most in-demand actor in Hollywood. But his post-2000s career has been more hit-and-miss: his latest straight-to-Netflix thriller The Whisper Man was slated by critics (the Guardian accused him of “sleepwalking” through the movie). His 2025 mob film The Alto Knights also landed badly. His first TV lead, in Netflix thriller Zero Day, in which he played a former US president, received mixed reviews. The last clear hit was 2023’s Killers of the Flower Moon, in which De Niro played an ageing cattle rancher orchestrating a series of murders of Osage tribe members; it is no coincidence the project reunited him with Scorsese for the first time since The Irishman in 2019.

Early 70s breakout

Born in Manhattan in 1943 and raised in Greenwich Village, De Niro’s parents Virginia Admiral and Robert De Niro Senior were prominent abstract expressionist painters and poets (they separated when De Niro was two and his dad came out as gay). Initially a shy child, he starred in a school production of The Wizard of Oz aged 10, which helped develop his confidence. He dropped out of high school aged 16 to study acting and took his first paid role that same year in a production of Chekhov’s The Bear. Delivering food and doing extra work to bring in money while auditioning and landing bit part roles, he secured his breakout in Mean Streets in 1973, the first of ten films he made with Scorsese, who grew up in the same New York neighbourhood as De Niro. His role as ‘Johnny Boy’ Civello was a meteoric success, both critically and at the box office, establishing De Niro’s reputation for depicting violent men.

The year Robert De Niro met Nobu

His method acting style would go on to be filtered through a raft of intense, highly physical roles before he softened a little in the late-1990s, shifting towards more comedic parts, such as retired CIA counterintelligence officer Jacky Byrnes in Meet the Parents.

Two significant turning points happened in 1988: De Niro met chef Nobu, and that same year the actor first pushed away from action and into light comedy with the release of Midnight Run (Nobu took six years to come around to opening a restaurant called ‘Nobu’, which eventually launched in 1994).

Two weeks after my interview, I book into the restaurant at Nobu Portman Square. It feels slightly less exciting entering the imposing glass building this time, but only a bit: it really is a stunning place. I order chef Nobu’s signature omakase menu, on which many of the dishes haven’t changed since the 1990s, including the superlative black cod miso that he popularised during the restaurant’s heyday. House music plays as I eat my way through salmon tartare with caviar and a tiny Japanese wakamomo peach. The glamorous, moody interior is softened by floor-to-ceiling views of the trees outside. If there’s anything to criticise, it is the service, which is not at the level you’d expect.

Can I remind you he is 83?

The brand’s impending push into the wellness space feels on-the-nose, given the age of the men behind it. What does wellness look like to a man like De Niro, especially given conversations surrounding longevity? He’s explaining that he’s keen to visit the site in Rutland but hasn’t been yet, when an agitated PR runs in from the other room to close down this topic of conversation. My questions have been heavily vetted and I’ve been instructed to speak only about the Egyptian hotel launches. Time for my final question, she says, despite there still being a quarter of my interview left. The question doesn’t appear to bother De Niro, though. After I finish recording, instead of bolting, he walks past the publicists to shake my hand and tell me to “take care”.

Unlike stars half his age, who tend to disappear into waiting Mercs to the airport, De Niro goes from our interview to a conference to talk about the Nobu projects in Egypt. Then he had a cocktail reception. Then, in the evening, he has dinner with 30 or 40 journalists and industry figures. In the foyer before the conference, property writers more used to penning dry business-to-business stories could barely contain their excitement at a chance to spot such a huge star. When it comes to promoting a brand, this level of commitment is practically unheard of. Can I remind you that he is 83?

Staying active into old age embodies a Japanese concept called ‘ikigai’, which chef Nobu himself practices. At 77, some years he still travels for 10 months out of the twelve. Perhaps De Niro’s dedication to Nobu – meeting journalists, architects and business people, scoping out new developments – is his way of keeping the lights on.

“Rogue” OpenAI agents have been blamed for helping knock a Wikipedia service offline, the latest in a string of incidents involving the ChatGPT maker’s increasingly autonomous technology.

The Wikimedia Foundation said agents it believes were operated by OpenAI flooded its platforms with millions of automated requests, crawled millions of pages and made hundreds of thousands of queries.

The activity may have contributed to a partial outage of its Wikidata Query Service on 7 May, according to the non-profit organisation behind Wikipedia.

But Wikimedia said the agents went beyond simply harvesting data, making unauthorised edits to its sites and attempting to access other services.

“We are deeply concerned about the impact of ‘rogue’ AI agents on platforms like ours”, the foundation said.

OpenAI is already facing questions over how well it can control increasingly autonomous AI systems after a series of security incidents.

In July, an OpenAI agent breached AI developer platform Hugging Face after escaping the confines of a testing environment.

The company has since uncovered unexpected activity involving other organisations, including Australian government websites, and said it has notified more than 100 organisations as it investigates its agents’ behaviour.

OpenAI has also disclosed cases in which models concealed mistakes, acted without permission and found unexpected ways around instructions during testing.

The company delayed the release of its latest AI model following safety concerns and said it was spending more than $500,000 (£376,913) a day reviewing past activity for further unintended behaviour.

‘New normal’

Wikimedia said its investigations found OpenAI agents had made millions of automated requests to its public APIs and crawled millions of pages.

Almost all of their unauthorised Wikipedia edits were tests made away from ordinary readers.

However, several changes to a citation tool were considered “potentially malicious” and appeared designed to use it as a middleman to retrieve information from elsewhere.

Agents also targeted Etherpad, a collaborative note-taking service used by the Wikimedia community, although Wikimedia said there was no evidence its systems or data had been compromised.

The foundation warned the growing use of autonomous agents were placing additional costs on organisations forced to investigate their activity and protect infrastructure from unexpected behaviour.

“This intense pressure on our infrastructure not only adds costs for servers and humans, but if left unaddressed, can block human visitors by overloading systems and causing outages”, it said.

Wider safety row inside OpenAI

Safety leader David Robinson quit last month after three and a half years at the company, arguing its “culture is broken” and that companies developing frontier AI were not being “nearly careful enough”.

OpenAI has separately fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling sensitive company information, including a safety researcher who worked with outside organisations investigations the Hugging Face breach.

Chief executive Sam Altman has defended the company’s broader approach, arguing that society should accept some “bad things” happening as the tech develops in return for its benefits.

“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying we will make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams or all the other bad things that will happen”, he said in an interview last week.

Wikimedia, however, said organisations maintaining the infrastructure that AI agents rely on should not be expected to absorb the consequences.

“We should not allow this behaviour to become the ‘new normal’ for the people or organisations that maintain it”, it said.

OpenAI said it appreciated Wikimedia’s “detailed findings” and was working with the organisation to analyse the activity.

“We’ll continue to share relevant information as that work progresses”, said spokesperson Drew Pusateri.

Why the next phase of direct lending will reward discipline over scale.

Private credit has enjoyed a remarkable run. Once a niche corner of finance, the asset class has expanded into a mainstream source of funding for private equity-backed businesses.

But as the market matures, the rules are changing. Rapid growth has brought greater scrutiny, a small number of highly publicised defaults, particularly in the US, and concerns about underwriting standards.

Indeed, the market is becoming more selective, with the strongest lenders focusing on relationships, diversification and the quality of the deals they choose to finance.

Here are three ways the next phase of direct lending is taking shape.

1. Scale is no longer the only measure of success

For much of the past 15 years, private credit managers have been focused on the size of their funds and the amount of capital they deployed. The value of assets under management has grown from around $380bn in 2010 to approximately $2.3tn today. The market is projected to reach $4.5tn by 2030.

However, as fund sizes and transactions have increased, investors have started asking more searching questions about underwriting standards and realised returns. Raising capital is no longer sufficient on its own. Managers also need to show they can deploy it carefully and generate consistent returns.

This is particularly important in the large-cap market, where a limited number of attractive deals can attract intense competition between lenders. When several providers are chasing the same transaction, pricing and leverage can overshadow the quality of the underlying credit.

That competitive pressure has already affected terms. Median private credit margins narrowed from 6.5 per cent at the start of 2023 to less than five per cent in 2025.

Investors must increasingly look beyond headline AUM and ask whether a manager has protected returns by knowing when to walk away.

2. The lower mid-market is becoming more attractive

Large private equity transactions tend to attract the most attention, but the lower mid-market is emerging as one of the more interesting areas for direct lenders.

These are businesses that are smaller than the household-name deals dominating financial headlines, but they can still offer strong growth prospects and resilient underlying businesses.

The financing dynamics are different, too. In the large-cap market, lenders often compete by offering lower pricing, higher leverage or looser terms. In the lower mid-market, there is greater focus on flexibility, local knowledge and a lender’s ability to support a company as it grows. This can create a better risk-reward balance.

For lenders, the lower mid-market offers the opportunity to negotiate more attractive pricing and protections, partly because competition is less intense. For sponsors, the right financing partner can provide more than a loan: it can offer acquisition finance, foreign exchange support, hedging and additional capital for future expansion.

Investec recently supported CBPE Capital’s investment in Brookbanks, a multidisciplinary consultancy, with senior debt facilities designed to give the business flexibility to develop and grow.

It also created a bespoke financing package for Triple Private Equity’s acquisitions of Derivia Intelligence, Extel and Euromoney. The package combined acquisition finance at operating-company level with a fund finance facility, alongside hedging and foreign exchange support.

However, this part of the market is not easy to serve well. Underwriting a smaller business can require much the same work as underwriting a larger one, while generating a smaller fee. That means lenders need deep origination networks and efficient processes to review a high volume of opportunities.

Investec reviews around 600 financing opportunities each year before completing approximately 25 to 30 new deals. That breadth allows us to be selective. 

3. Europe’s fragmented market could reward discipline

Private credit is often discussed as if it were a single, uniform market. In reality, it is made up of different regions, strategies and borrower types, each with its own risks.

The recent pressure points have been most visible in the US, particularly among semi-liquid and interval funds that have grown rapidly. Those vehicles are less prevalent in Europe, where the market has a different structure.

European private credit has an estimated $400bn in assets under management, and non-bank lenders account for around 12 per cent of the region’s lending market. That leaves significant room for further growth.

Europe’s fragmentation can be a complication, but it can also be an opportunity for lenders with the right expertise. Businesses operate across different legal systems, languages and restructuring frameworks. A financing approach that works in the UK may not translate directly to France, Germany or the Benelux. Lenders that understand those differences are better placed to provide financing that is appropriate to the needs of businesses operating in each market.

That makes relationships and infrastructure increasingly important. The strongest lenders will not necessarily be the ones with the largest balance sheets. They will be the ones able to work across multiple markets, assess them consistently and provide certainty when a transaction needs to move quickly.

Diversification is also central to that model. Direct lending returns are capped on the upside, meaning a single write-off can have a significant impact. Unlike equity investing, where a small number of exceptional deals can drive performance, lenders need to protect the portfolio as a whole.

According to industry data, direct lending defaults stood at 1.4 per cent, compared with 2.6 per cent for high-yield bonds and 3.6 per cent for broadly syndicated loans.

The figures do not remove the risks. Geopolitical uncertainty, higher borrowing costs and disruption in sectors such as software could still lead to more distressed loans. But they do suggest that concerns about private credit need to be considered in context.

Conclusion: The next phase will favour quality over quantity

Capital will continue to flow into private credit, particularly as private equity sponsors seek flexible sources of finance and banks remain selective about balance-sheet lending.

But the market is entering a more mature phase. AUM growth and deployment alone will matter less than underwriting discipline, the strength of borrower relationships and the consistency of realised returns.

The lenders best placed to succeed will be those with the infrastructure to review large numbers of opportunities, the expertise to operate across European markets and the discipline to say no when a deal does not meet their standards.

In private credit’s next chapter, sustainable growth will depend on something more difficult to measure: knowing when not to lend.

Despite developing an early taste for Tè Bheag, the blended Scotch bottled by the late Sir Ian Noble on Skye, Paddy Fletcher spent the first 15 years of his career in journalism, accountancy, housebuilding and technology startups. It wasn’t until his mid-thirties that he ventured North to co-found Port of Leith Distillery with school friend Ian Stirling. 

On leaving Durham University with an economics degree, Paddy became a reporter at Risk Magazine, where he wrote about the alphabet soup of financial instruments – RMBS, CDO, CDO2, CDS – which three years later triggered the 2008 financial crash. He quit journalism and, following an MSc in economic history at the London School of Economics, joined the accountancy firm BDO. “That was a bit like doing an MBA, but being paid to do it,” says Paddy.

When he and Ian were sharing a flat in London, they began getting seriously into Scotch, initially as hobbyists. They attended tastings and even built a whisky still in their back garden. 

“What frustrated us at the time was all the interesting and innovative things in whisky seemed to be happening in Tasmania, Sweden, and Brooklyn – not in Scotland”. Even as they vowed to do something to address this, Paddy’s next career move was to ride-hailing app Hailo. Having raised £120m from investors, the app was being rolled out internationally. “Everything was on fire… My main job was to work out when we were going to run out of cash”. 

The pair were hatching a plan to build a Scotch whisky distillery as Paddy moved between London-based finance roles with startups including YPlan and WeWork, while Ian was working in retail and international sales at Kensington-based wine merchants Robeson Wine.

They revisited their maths and double-checked their sums after a meeting with Mark Reynier, fresh from the £58m sale of Bruichladdich, who somewhat brutally told them: “Everything you know about whisky is wrong, you’ve got no idea what you’re doing and this business plan’s a joke.”

Paddy has been able to apply some of the lessons he had learned in tech startups to the whisky business. “Seeing startups from the inside meant I could watch where the mistakes were being made – and work out how to avoid them.” 

Soon afterwards they set up Muckle Brig Ltd to launch their distillery, and signed a lease on a one-third-of-an-acre site overlooking Leith Docks’ Western Harbour and the Royal Yacht Britannia. But they soon realised they’d have to buy the plot to have credibility with investors.

So why did they choose such a restricted site, where building a distillery was almost certain to be difficult and expensive?

“The whole point was that everyone was building sheds in the Highlands [as whisky distilleries] but that’s a me-too product. If you’re playing in the Scotch whisky game, you’re playing against 800lb gorilla organisations with legacy, heritage, tradition, stock, consumers – none of which you can chip away at.”

Buying the land, constructing the nine-storey tower, and purchasing the distilling equipment came to £15m – more than envisaged. However, it seems to be working. Even though it still lacks a single malt, the Port of Leith Distillery had 100,000 visitors through the door last year. 

Paddy Fletcher explains that the Port of Leith Distillery brand has been reserved for their single malt (due to launch in October 2027), while other products come under Muckle Brig subsidiaries Leith Bond (independent bottlers) and Lind & Lime (a gin brand launched in 2018).

He says Fraser Thornton, the former Burn Stewart MD who joined Muckle Brig as a non-exec in 2022, and became its chairman in 2025, has been an invaluable sounding board. “He latched onto the enthusiasm that Ian and I had for the category, and for what we were trying to do, and helped ensure we don’t do dumb things.”

As we savour our table whiskies and admire the panoramic views of the Firth of Forth, Paddy reflects on the challenges facing the sector, which has lately been buffeted by overstocking, reduced production, and geopolitical and energy-price shocks such as Donald Trump’s war on Iran.

O n 17 December 1903, one of the most significant stretches of time in human history was measured near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. That time was 12 seconds – the length for the first flight of a powered aircraft, the Wright Flyer. By the end of the day that number had risen to 59 seconds. Most of us know at least some of that story, but what fewer know is that the timer for that all-important fifth of a minute was a Gallet ‘Sun’ stopwatch.

Indeed, Gallet isn’t a brand widely known outside of die-hard vintage circles, despite having some famous fans over the years. The 33rd President of the USA, Harry S Truman, wore a Gallet Flying Officer, a pilots’ worldtimer designed to display refuelling stops. F1 legend Jim Clark wore the Gallet MultiChron 12H racing chronograph. 

Unfortunately, like the rest of the Swiss watch industry it was hit hard by the quartz crisis of the 1970s and 80s. It staggered on longer than most, but by the mid-90s, a surging Swiss franc killed off any competitiveness it had left and it shuttered its doors in 1994. Still, those early days of Gallet have the kind of horological heritage you just can’t buy… unless you’re Breitling.

Having re-launched the iconic heritage watchmaker Universal Genève with a huge drop of modernised reissues, the brand had recruited what it called a ‘Board of Collectors’ to steer them towards genuinely interesting watch brands. One name kept coming up: Gallet.

“Gallet instantly appealed,” says Rossignol. “It was launched in 1826, so this year is actually its 200th anniversary, and it has an incredibly rich archive. It was a pioneer in its field and shared roots with Breitling without being a copy-paste. It was a leader in chronographs; it built instruments for professional aviation and racing and yet it wasn’t as well-known as we – and many collectors – feel it should have been.”

Gallet vs Breitling

So how does one differentiate a specialist in aviation chronographs like Gallet from a specialist in aviation chronographs like Breitling? Apparently, with a sense of adventure. While Gallet doesn’t currently have its own spaces yet, it is piggybacking on Breitling’s, meaning that if you go into a Breitling store, you’ll find what looks like a well-heeled safari lodge doubling as a watch shop. Think white canvas, greens and orange (taken, incidentally, from an early Flying Officer model), a kind of wilderness chic that nails the new incarnation of Gallet perfectly. Even its ambassadors are off the beaten track, with nature photographer Donal Boyd, paragliding influencer Benjamin Kellett and climber adventurer L Renee Blount. 

Branding however is only window dressing without a decent range of watches and on that front Gallet has gone hard. There are four new collections, comprising 11 new watches, which is a punchy starting point – and honestly, it’s very convincing.

First, there’s the Flying Officer. This is Gallet’s most famous reference and the one worn by Truman. As mentioned earlier, it was originally designed to show all the necessary refuelling stops a pilot might need, which in the days of much more efficient flight, isn’t really necessary. Instead, it’s been redesigned into a 40mm, military heritage-style worldtimer, swapping practical destinations for far-flung, adventurous locales that suit the brand’s new safari style. It’s available in a practical black and a lovely light blue.

A bigger departure from Gallet canon is that the Flying Officer is also available as a time-only version, sans chronograph, in orange or dark blue. It brings the price down and is otherwise identical, though it does feel like a misstep. Generally, more options are always better, but it’s doubtful many on Breitling’s ‘Board of Collectors’ suggested the idea.

Next-up, the Multichron, which comes in two different flavours. On the one hand there’s the classic aviation-inspired chronograph version, the 42mm Multichron Pilot with a rotating bezel and telemeter and second timezone; on the other, the 41mm Multichron Sport with a tachymeter on the dial periphery and a slim bezel. The former is a classic vintage chronograph with mushroom pushers and a rugged, textured dial; the latter is sleeker and sportier, with elongated button pushers and a more refined dial. Both come in black and blue with contrasting subdials for a very similar execution but distinctive feels.

All of the Flying Officer and Multichron models are equipped with the Sellita SW510 (renamed the Gallet 23) with a solid 65-hour power reserve and they’re all priced at £3,400 on strap, £3,600 on a bracelet. That’s the same across the board – other than those Sellita SW200-equipped time-only models, which sit at £2,200. It’s an interesting approach and means that the choice comes down to style rather than price variance within the collection. The same goes for the straps, where you can choose any strap you like, and extras will set you back £70 regardless of material. Yes, you can get much more accessible Sellita-equipped chronographs, but Gallet’s line-up has heritage style to spare and the respectable backing of being ‘manufactured by Breitling’, which is stamped on every caseback.

“We’re not trying to be a carbon copy of Breitling,” says Rossignol. “For us, ‘manufactured by Breitling’ is a seal of quality. It’s one of the leading Swiss manufacturers and being able to leverage that is a way of assuring collectors of our quality – as long as we don’t start just making Breitling watches.”

This kind of relationship isn’t new. In fact, when Tudor was launched in 1946, founder Hans Wilsdorf stated that its quality would be guaranteed by Rolex. This idea, having a more accessibly priced brand using much of the same infrastructure, has striking similarities with Breitling and Gallet.

Gallet deep cuts

While the Breitling-Gallet dynamic is more about assembly in Gallet’s main collection, there is one line that’s a bit more involved: the Gallet Classics Collection. This is a triplet of chronographs that evoke some of Gallet’s most famous yet least commercial historical models: The Multichron 45, the regatta-ready Yachting Big Eye and the Silverlight.

Not only are two of them archival deep cuts – despite its monochrome vintage looks, the Silverlight is actually a completely new reference – but all three have Breitling’s own B09 Hand-Wound movement. This is the same chronograph used in Breitling’s own collection and is a cut above Sellita, with an extended 70-hour power reserve – and thus an extended price of £5,300. Even though they’re slightly more expensive, these smaller, 38mm models are the pieces most collectors will want.

Gallet’s launch is officially part of what Breitling insists on calling the House of Brands. And while it sounds like a department store discount basement, it does present a solid run of watches, from stone dialled Polerouters at the top to fun, historical chronographs at the bottom. Yet while they might be at the lower end of the list, for me Gallet has the most potential.

“It started as us meeting a need amongst collectors,” says Rossignol. “But once we decided on Gallet, once we started looking into what we could do with this brand, it became so much more. Now we have a genuinely exciting range of watches and an opportunity to introduce people to a fantastic watchmaking heritage.

    The Donkervoort P24 RS is simultaneously one of the fastest and slowest cars I have ever driven. The flyweight 600hp roadster can rocket to 60mph in circa. 2.5 seconds and pull 2.4G in the corners. And yet… every time you stop for fuel or a flat white, you need to factor in time for chatting with strangers who want to take photos and quiz you about this singular vehicle.

    David Beckham could pull up at the opposite pump in a new Lamborghini Revuelto and he’d be practically invisible. So, to save Donkervoort drivers from further delays when filling up, I will attempt to answer the many questions I was asked during a morning with the P24 RS. Starting with: “What the hell is a Donkervoort?”

    While the name is little known here, Donkervoort has been building cars in its native Holland since 1978. It all began when Joop Donkervoort went on a school trip to Britain and spotted a Lotus Seven: the lightweight sports car that lives on today as the Caterham Seven. The youthful Joop fell instantly in love and, when his studies were finished, he set about becoming the official Dutch importer for Lotus.

    It transpired that the rather rudimentary Seven couldn’t be homologated for sale in Holland, but Joop was undeterred. He redesigned the car to satisfy local legislation, making it more comfortable and usable in the process. The first Donkervoort had arrived. 

    Donkervoort’s cars have grown ever faster and more technically advanced, but the ethos of the back-to-basics Lotus is still woven into its DNA. You see it in the open front wheels, manual transmission and front-engined, rear-driven layout of the P24 RS. This is a Seven turned up to 11. 

    Earlier Donkervoorts used Ford engines, from the humble Pinto to the legendary Cosworth YB, then the company switched to Audi power from 1999. However, emissions rules mean time is running out for the charismatic five-cylinder motor – borrowed from the Audi RS3, and boosted to 500hp in the outgoing F22 roadster – so Donkervoort has returned to its roots, bolting in the 3.5-litre V6 from the Ford GT supercar.   

    A dial on the centre console offers a choice of Comfort, Touring and Performance modes, uncorking 400hp, 500hp or 600hp respectively. Combined with a dry weight of just 780kg (call it 840kg with fluids), that gives the P24 RS a power-to-weight ratio to shame most supercars. The latest Porsche 911 GT3 RS, for example, musters 525hp and tips the scales at 1,450kg. 

    Donkervoort plans to build 150 examples of the P24 RS, 100 of them painted and 50 in naked carbon fibre, and the company’s loyal fanbase means the majority have already been sold. The big news for Brits, though, is that this is the first ever Donkervoort offered in right-hand drive. As sales officer Quentin Mond points out, it will open up other RHD markets as well, including Japan and Australia.

    The car’s body and front subframe are made from a patented material called Ex-Core, which sandwiches a layer of expanding foam between two pieces of carbon fibre and cures them together in an aluminium mould. Developed by Donkervoort, the technology is now licensed to several F1 teams, as well as being used in aircraft and luxury yachts, delivering light weight and huge torsional rigidity. 

    The Donkervoort rides on double wishbone suspension

    The P24 RS rides on double wishbone suspension with Tractive adaptive dampers that remove the need for anti-roll bars. Its brakes are lightened discs (carbon-ceramics are optional) with four-piston AP Racing calipers. The wheels are 18-inch forged rims at the front and 19s at the rear, wrapped in bespoke Nankang semi-slick tyres.  

    As you might expect, this kind of performance and exclusivity doesn’t come cheap. When the P24 RS is launched here in 2028 – coinciding with Donkervoort’s 50th anniversary – it will cost £302,400. Serious supercar money, in other words. UK sales are via Premier GT in West Sussex, or you can choose to buy one direct from the factory. 

    Nailing its hardcore credentials to the wall, the options available for a P24 RS include power steering, anti-lock brakes (ABS) and air conditioning. You can also tailor the specification to your taste, with finishes such as the green-tinted carbon fibre seen here. “Every one of the 150 cars will be unique,” explains Mond. “There is no such thing as a typical Donkervoort owner.”

    Closer inspection reveals a high standard of fit and finish, from the alignment of the carbon fibre weave between body panels to the plush, leather-lined interior

    This particular P24 RS also sports the bolt-on Aero Package. Made from Ex-Core and yours for £17,000, it adds up to 180kg of downforce via an enormous, snowplough-like front splitter, side skirts and dainty hoop spoilers behind each of the rear wheels. Best to combine it with the suspension lift kit (£7,660), mind, or you risk becoming beached at the first hint of a speed hump.

    The P24 RS is “a beast even by Donkervoort standards,” says Mond. It looks suitably intimidating, too – like a praying mantis ready to strike. I’m also reminded of a die-cast Hot Wheels toy rendered at 100 percent scale, or perhaps a Transformer before it switches into a robot. Ultimately, this is a car that looks like nothing else.  

    Closer inspection reveals a high standard of fit and finish, from the alignment of the carbon fibre weave between body panels to the plush, leather-lined interior. A Lotus Seven-esque kit car this is not. 

    If it didn’t already look striking enough, lifting the Donkervoort’s dihedral doors is guaranteed to draw a crowd. My favourite design detail, though, has to be the pop-out LED headlights, which pivot upwards from either side of the nose cone when switched on, and look like an additional pair of aerodynamic winglets.

    Swivelling your hips over the broad sill requires a certain dexterity, although you can unclip the steering wheel, racing car-style, to make access easier. Once ensconced, the carbon-shelled Recaro seats are remarkably roomy and the driving position offers plenty of adjustment, even if the four-point harnesses are a faff. I’d swap them for conventional seat belts if you plan to use your P24 RS for road trips, rather than as a track toy. 

    Indeed, Mond says this is very much a road car, estimating that only around 10 per cent of owners take part in track days. “I know at least three people who have a Donkervoort as their only car and drive it daily,” he adds. “The boot holds 298 litres, so you can definitely use it for touring over long distances.”

    You sit low with the wheel pulled close to your chest and legs tucked inside a narrow footwell. A small screen displays the essential driving data, but there are no other distractions: just a few eyeball air vents, a stubby manual gear lever and the bright red PTC controller. No stability control either. Gulp. Let’s start off in Comfort mode, shall we?

    At first, driving the Donkervoort feels a bit alien. You can see the front wheels, for starters, and like a Morgan or Caterham, there’s a sense of being atop the rear axle with the majority of the car stretched out ahead. Thankfully, this P24 RS has the electromechanical power steering option because a) it’s direct and full of detail, and b) I suspect it would be a workout without it. 

    The shift lever is notchy and heavy, and the pedal positioning makes it tricky to heel-and-toe, but there is an auto-blip function if you want to cheat. As in the Ford GT, the Ecoboost V6 inhales the road with a furious whoosh of turbocharged boost, interrupted by gasps of escaping air when you snatch the next gear. It’s intense and industrial, rather than tuneful or evocative like the old Audi five-pot.  

    By God, though, it’s quick. The 400hp setting merely feels fast, but step up to 500hp Touring mode and things suddenly get altogether more serious. The five-speed gearbox’s ratios are exceptionally long – second gear does the job around town and on tighter country lanes – yet acceleration is still utterly explosive. With so little weight, the Donkervoort gathers speed like it’s been dropped from a plane without a parachute.

    Maximum-attack Performance mode

    I’ll confess, I only switched into maximum-attack Performance mode for a few minutes, wary of the lack of stability systems and my sub-Max Verstappen level of driving talent.  Here, as with many modern supercars, you encounter the kind of performance that is hard to deploy on a public road. It’s an onslaught on the senses, but one that demands a cool head and a calm pair of hands. In the midst of a heatwave, with the roof open and no air-con (not an option fitted to this P24 RS), it feels a bit beyond my skill set.     

    There is much to enjoy here without going at silly speeds, though. The Donkervoort is unashamedly analogue, a car that demands your attention, even when you are just pottering through villages at 20mph. From its feathery steering to its lithe body control, you feel intimately involved with every input. Heading home in my family SUV later felt like driving with my limbs inside several layers of bubble wrap. 

    That sense of connection swiftly builds your confidence, too. You can sense the lack of the weight over the front wheels and feel the rubber bite as you turn in. And at the rear, a Torsen differential provides a crisp, mechanical link between the engine and the driven wheels, allowing you to trim the car’s line using the throttle – or flick it sideways, should the mood take you. 

    If you’re the sort of person who feels supercars have gone a bit soft, the P24 RS could be just the tonic

    Guiding the Donkervoort along wet, winter roads would doubtless be very different, requiring a delicacy akin to handling a live grenade. But in an era where cars increasingly feel like appliances, one that makes every drive an experience, and makes driving an end in itself, is to be applauded.  

    As I handed back the keys, half of me ached for another go, while the other was thankful to have returned the car in one piece, and really fancied a lie-down, thank you very much. As you will have gathered by now, this is a car of contrasts. It takes a familiar formula to extremes that would have been unimaginable all those years ago, when Joop Donkervoort first laid eyes on a Lotus Seven.

    If you’re the sort of person who feels supercars have gone a bit soft, the P24 RS could be just the tonic. Just don’t expect to travel anywhere very quickly – even if a few more Brits now know what the hell a Donkervoort is.

    On the issues, the Tories are marginally ahead of Reform on who is best to reduce the cost of living and strengthen the economy, but on both fronts Burnham’s Labour Party is now significantly ahead. Reform beats everyone on who is best to reduce migration, while Labour’s relative strengths are building housing, improving wages and job security and health and social care. This effectively leaves the Tories squeezed from all sides, without a significant lead on any issue.

    Andrew Griffith’s appointment as shadow chancellor last month led to renewed attacks on the Tories’ record. Labour quickly pointed out that Griffith was a Treasury minister during Liz Truss’ mini-budget to undermine the opposition’s credibility, even though Griffith said he hadn’t seen it until the night before.

    What are voters’ main concerns?

    The City AM / Freshwater Strategy Poll asked last month what voters’ main concerns would be about voting for the Conservative Party. Overall, the top concern was that they cannot be trusted to keep their promises (35 per cent), followed by their record on the NHS (30 per cent). The handling of the economy while in government came in third (29 per cent). A separate question found the electorate evenly split on how well they remember the mini-budget, with 49 per cent saying well, and 47 per cent saying not well. 

    But there are splits in interesting ways among voters. The economy is more likely to be a reason not to vote Tory among centrist and centre left voters, including Lib Dems (42 per cent) and Labour voters (38 per cent), but matters far less to Reform (28 per cent) or Tory (19 per cent) backers. Voters on the right are most likely to cite their record on immigration as a main concern. We have new policies, new plans, new people coming on board.” This reflects the central challenge for the Tories: presenting a credible alternative, one that people not only back in principle, but one that is shown to be actually deliverable, a leadership that can deliver it, and together is a meaningful break from the past.

    After years in which central-bank backstops encouraged Eurozone investors to look the other way, the bond market has finally started to notice, writes Helen Thomas

    Fifteen years after the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis, its old fault lines are beginning to reappear. Political risk is rising across Europe just as global bond markets are selling off. That is a toxic combination for highly indebted, low-growth governments whose finances become progressively less sustainable as borrowing costs rise.

    France is now the weakest link. The spread between French and German 10-year government bonds has widened to around 150 basis points, levels not seen since the sovereign debt crisis. Back then, higher bond yields threatened to trigger a self-reinforcing doom loop. Rising sovereign borrowing costs damaged the value of government bonds held by domestic banks; weaker banks increased the prospective burden on governments; investors demanded still higher yields.

    Membership of the euro made the adjustment particularly brutal. A country could neither devalue its currency nor set its own interest rate. Instead it had to restore competitiveness through politically painful fiscal and economic adjustment. Ironically this now leaves the so-called peripheral PIGS (Portugal, Italy, Greece and Spain) in a stronger position looking forward. It is the core countries that are now posing existential questions for the European project.

    France intends to issue a record €340bn of medium and long-term government bonds next year. Germany’s debt agency expects its own borrowing to exceed the record planned for 2026. Both countries have right-wing parties topping their polls and achieving greater electoral representation. Le Pen’s National Rally just gained enough representation in the Senate to be able to form a parliamentary group in the Upper House for the first time. The AfD came within three seats of an outright majority in the Saxony Anhalt regional election.

    And now Spain faces an early general election which could usher in a right-wing coalition government that might include the far right Vox party. Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has decided to go to the polls on 29th November rather than let the parliament run until next August, hoping he can capitalise on public outrage over housing scarcity that recently led to the eviction of an 87-year-old woman. Sanchez is the great political survivor and his country has at least experienced some growth in the last few years which has helped to reduce its deficit. But it increases the moment of peril by introducing more uncertainty to the Eurozone.

    The previous crisis involved a weak periphery threatening to contaminate a strong core. What happens when the core itself becomes the source of instability?

    France, after all, is not Greece. It is the Eurozone’s second-largest economy, a nuclear power and one of the founding political pillars of the European project. It may prove not merely too big to fail, but too big to bail.

    Except the European Central Bank (ECB) has something up its sleeve. In July 2022 it created the Transmission Protection Instrument, or TPI. Its purpose is ostensibly technical: to ensure that monetary policy is transmitted evenly through the Eurozone. If bond markets move in an “unwarranted” and “disorderly” manner such that financing conditions deteriorate beyond what economic fundamentals justify, the ECB can buy the affected country’s government bonds. Purchases are not restricted in size in advance.

    It is an ingenious construction. It is also exquisitely ambiguous. It is hard to judge when a repricing becomes disorderly rather than merely a reflection of shifting fundamentals. If investors demand a higher yield because a government has excessive debt, persistent deficits and unstable politics, is that an impairment of monetary transmission or simply the market doing its job?

    The distinction matters because European Monetary Union contains an unresolved contradiction. There is one central bank setting the price of money but national governments still control their own taxation and spending. The treaties prohibit the ECB from simply financing those governments.

    Hence the elaborate criteria attached to the TPI. The ECB must consider fiscal sustainability, macroeconomic imbalances and compliance with EU fiscal rules before intervening. Activation ultimately requires the Governing Council to make a judgement that intervention is proportionate to maintaining price stability.

    France demonstrates how murky this could become. It is currently subject to the EU’s Excessive Deficit Procedure. Yet in June the European Commission judged that France had taken “effective action” towards correcting its excessive deficit, meaning the procedure remains open but is currently held in abeyance. Under the ECB’s carefully worded TPI criteria, that leaves at least some wiggle room over how eligibility might ultimately be judged.

    So the firewall designed to reassure markets ultimately rests on judgement calls made by central bankers. And unlike Mario Draghi’s famous promise in 2012 to do “whatever it takes” to preserve the euro, the TPI has never been tested. When asked in July 2022 how it would operate, ECB President Lagarde waffled that “the decision to begin TPI purchases, as I said, will be in the entire discretion of the Governing Council. Now, clearly, to assess whether you have unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics, the Governing Council will take into account multiple indicators to determine the warranted versus unwarranted, and to determine the orderly versus disorderly, and multiple indicators have been discussed and will be taken into account by the Governing Council”.

    The ECB’s dilemma is becoming more acute because it is currently fighting inflation with higher interest rates. Those same rates worsen the debt arithmetic of highly indebted governments. Buying their bonds to suppress yields while raising interest rates to suppress inflation would be an uncomfortable balancing act. The alternative pressure valve is the euro itself. But a weaker currency raises imported inflation, potentially requiring still tighter monetary policy.

    Something, somewhere, therefore has to give.

    Europe’s citizens are becoming more politically rebellious. Its governments are becoming more indebted. And after years in which central-bank backstops encouraged investors to look the other way, the bond market has finally started to notice.

    The people are revolting. The question is whether the ECB can stop the bond market from joining them.

    Helen Thomas is CEO of Blonde Money

    TalkTalk was founded to take on BT, slash the price of broadband and shake up a market dominated by a handful of incumbents.

    But more than two decades later, the challenger has ended up in the arms of the company it was built to challenge.

    BT stepped in on Monday to buy Talktalk and its wholesale arm PlatformX Communications out of administration, ending months of increasingly urgent attempts to find a buyer for the debt-laden broadband provider.

    The deal keeps 1.5 million retail customers and another one million wholesale connections online, while around 900 employees will move across to BT.

    For customers, little changes for now; Broadband remains connected and contracts remain in place. But the deal caps a long decline from one of Britain’s biggest broadband challengers.

    Founded by Sir Charles Dunstone in 2003 as part of Carphone Warehouse, Talktalk grew rapidly by undercutting established players. It was spun out as a listed company in 2010 and had around four million customers by 2019.

    But cheap broadband becomes a difficult business when customers start disappearing and debts do not.

    Talktalk was taken private in 2021 by Dunstone and Toscafund in a deal valuing it at more than £1bn, before spending years trying to get its finances onto firmer ground.

    Repeated refinancings bought it time, including a £115m injection led by lender and shareholder Ares Management in February.

    But Talktalk remained loss-making despite generating around £1.2bn of revenue over the past year, while its customer base continued to shrink.

    By this summer, Octopus Investments entered talks over PlatformX, separate bidders circled the consumer arm and TalkTalk offloaded 120,000 customers to smaller rival Rise Fibre. However, no buyer emerged for the whole business.

    A rescue with winners and losers

    Allowing Talktalk simply to fail was hardly an attractive option. Its wholesale business supports services across healthcare, emergency services, transport, banking and government, alongside millions of household connections.

    BT chief executive Allison Kirkby called the situation “genuinely unprecedented”, while culture secretary Lisa Nandy warned a collapse risked disrupting vital public services.

    Talktalk was ultimately sold through a pre-pack administration, allowing BT to acquire the operating businesses immediately and debt-free.

    “When we hear the words ‘administration’ or ‘insolvency’, it can sound as though everything stops overnight, but that isn’t necessarily what happens”, Molly Monks, insolvency expert at Parker Walsh, said.

    The arrangement is less comfortable for creditors, who are left seeking repayment from Talktalk’s insolvent estate.

    BT, meanwhile, gains 1.5 million retail customers and one million wholesale connections.

    BT expects the deal to have a roughly £400m cash impact this financial year, although Bloomberg Intelligence’s Matthew Bloxham estimates the implied purchase price itself is below £240m before other costs and working capital.

    ‘A stich up’

    Talktalk was also a major customer of BT-owned Openreach, meaning the deal protects those network volumes while bringing its retail customers under the same roof.

    That has inevitably raised competition concerns within the market. Virgin Media branded the takeover a “stitch up masked as a rescue deal”, while Bloxham estimates BT’s fixed-broadband share could rise from around 29 per cent to 35 per cent.

    The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) now has until 19 October to examine the deal.

    For Talktalk customers, services, prices and contracts remain unchanged for now, with Monks warning against making a “knee-jerk decision” to cancel.

    The longer-term fate of the TalkTalk name is less certain, however, with Mayo Wynne Baxter parnter Nick Stockley saying it would not be surprising to see the brand gradually disappear as customers are moved into BT’s wider business.

    There would be a certain symmetry to that ending. TalkTalk spent more than two decades trying to loosen BT’s grip on British broadband and in the end, BT was the very company left to rescue it.

    Hundreds of new films will be premiered at this year’s festival, and many of the screenings are publicly bookable, with tickets currently on sale. New tickets for ‘sold out’ events are constantly being added to the website, so if an event looks sold out, check back again later in the week. 

    Screenings, many attended by the cast and crew of the films, as well as talks, events, art installations and immersive experiences all form parts of this year’s festival, which takes place in the capital between Wednesday 7 October to Sunday 18 October 2026. 

    Here are some of the best events to book this London Film Festival.

    London Film Festival 2026: the big tickets

    While some movies may show as sold out, new tickets are added regularly (daily and weekly) for some of the festival’s biggest releases. 

    Due to no-shows, standby tickets are also available on the day at the London Film Festival venues, so it can be worth showing up spontaneously to see what’s available (in fact, this is an approach the festival is publicising). 

    This year’s Opening Night Gala is Elsinore, a biographical drama starring Andrew Scott as Scottish actor Ian Charleson, who played Hamlet at the National Theatre in 1989 months before he passed away from AIDS. 

    The Closing Gala is The Debut, a musical comedy written and directed by Jesse Eisenberg. It follows an American housewife, played by Julianne Moore, who loses her sense of reality when she adopts the personality of another woman while playing a role in a local theatre production. 

    Artificial follows the story of Sam Altman

    Other big-hitters at this year’s festival to book include Artificial, from Call Me By Your Name director Luca Guadagnino. The film follows the life of Sam Altman, the founder of one of the biggest artificial intelligence platforms, Open AI.

    And hedonism is put under the microscope in Club Kid, a celebration of New York nightlife culture with a through line about one promoter whose partying is put on hold over the discovery that he has a son. 

    Fatherland is a stirring exploration of a father and daughter’s journey through postwar Germany. 

    The Mayor of London’s Gala is Ink, the new film from Danny Boyle following Rupert Murdoch’s newspaper career and the culture of Fleet Street during the era of the long, boozy lunch.

    It’s one of plenty taking the corporate world as its backdrop. Another is Prima Facie, the screen adaptation of Suzie Miller’s Olivier Award-winning West End play which originally starred Killing Eve actor Jodie Comer. 

    All About the Money follows a wealthy heir of a global enterprise conglomerate who sets up a communist camp in a rural part of America to campaign against the capitalist system he made his money within; Bunker is the story of an architect tasked with building a bunker for a tech billionaire.

    London Film Festival talks to book

    Many of the screen talks have already sold out, although there are still tickets left for Slumdog Millionaire director Danny Boyle’s on 16 October.

    A range of less high profile talks are free to attend, including one on how stories in film create change, a conversation with disability advocate Adam Pearson and a discussion about editing the auteur. 

    A range of free-to-attend DJ nights are also scheduled for the weekends during the festival at the BfI bar on the Southbank.

    The NHS may not be able to replace Palantir before a crunch deadline on its £330m data contract, raising the stakes for ministers as pressure mounts to cut ties with the US tech giant.

    The warning comes as ministers weigh Palantir’s future and campaigners ramp up pressure to ditch the company, with more than 44,000 people lodging formal objections to their data being processed through the platform.

    The company said its customers use open-source frameworks including Python and Apache Spark, describing interoperability as a “core Palantir design principle”.

    But the government has admitted the practical timetable for replacing the FDP could prove more difficult.

    In a letter to the Health and Social Care Committee seen by City AM, health minister James Frith said officials were still assessing the “continuity and reliability” of the service.

    “If it is determined that a successor contract is required… due to timelines required for normal government procurement processes it is unlikely that a new contract could be in place by March”, he said.

    Palantir hits back over NHS benefits

    The looming decision comes amid a separate row over whether the platform is delivering what taxpayers were promised.

    The NHS Chief Data Officers Network recently said the FDP had been “unable to demonstrate the level of evidence, confidence and realised value expected”.

    Palantir pushed back, pointing to government estimates that the platform will deliver £808m of benefits and £4.92 for every £1 spent.

    It says trusts using its software had recorded over 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3 per cent reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients and a 5.8 per cent average improvement against the NHS’s 28-day Faster Cancer Diagnosis Standard.

    Last Friday, over 44,000 people used Article 21 of UK data protection law to object to their information being processed through the FDP.

    But the company stressed it acts las a data processor, while NHS bodies remain the controllers of whether information is used and for how long.

    “Palantir does not have access to data beyond what our customers authorise”, the company told City AM.
